narrate.summary: The paper develops a theory for how far mobile sensors may need to move when a signal model changes and the D-optimal sensor placement is recomputed. It considers a fixed mobility graph and determinant-based placement objectives built from a changing subspace projector. The authors measure movement by matching old and new sensor positions to minimize the greatest travel distance, and define a distance margin to quantify how much worse distant placements are under the old objective. They prove that sufficiently small projector changes and a sufficiently large distance margin ensure every new optimum stays within a chosen radius. A weighted-path example shows that perturbation size and eigengap alone cannot guarantee small movement; the paper also gives finite certification methods and extensions to other determinant criteria.
narrate.key_results: In the synthetic study, 1,189 of 1,224 one-edge perturbation cases, or 97.1%, met the theorem’s conditions for certification, and the observed movement never exceeded the certified radius in those cases. A nontrivial certificate was obtained in 1,035 cases, or 87.0%; the certified and actual radii were equal in 561 cases, or 47.2%, including 547 cases with no movement. The optimizer moved in 33 eligible cases, and the median gap between certified and actual movement was two hops overall and one hop among cases with positive movement. In a separate example, actual movement was one hop while the certified radius was four hops; the paper cautions that the synthetic cases do not support ranking graph families.

key_equations.name: Distance-margin movement guarantee
key_equations.explanation: Here M_t(P) is the distance margin at time t for radius P, B_t is the perturbation budget, d_match is the bottleneck matching distance, S*_t is a baseline maximizing placement, and S is any maximizing placement after the update; the implication states that a margin exceeding the budget confines every new maximizer to radius P.

narrate.limitations_stated: The movement measure treats sensors as interchangeable and does not account for sensor types, trajectory collisions, travel times, or edge-capacity constraints. The experiments use small synthetic instances and exhaustive evaluation, and the authors note that the certificate can be conservative and that computing margins by enumeration limits its use on larger networks. The guarantees concern exact maximizers and local-region feasibility, not whether a particular placement algorithm finds the global optimum.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The stability guarantee depends on the chosen subspace model and objective; real sensor data may not be represented well by the assumed projector, and the paper does not validate the guarantees on field measurements. The numerical study covers a limited set of small graph families and perturbation scenarios, so its reported certification frequencies may not predict performance in operational sensor networks.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose finding conservative lower bounds on distance margins without enumerating all placements, to make certification practical on larger networks. They also suggest extending the movement geometry to heterogeneous sensors, travel costs, and collision constraints, and extending the stability results to approximate maximizers produced by practical algorithms.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the certificates on real dynamic sensing applications and assess whether the assumed projector drift reflects model changes observed in practice. Further work could also study sequential placement updates with operational constraints, including sensor-specific movement limits and measurement availability during relocation.

narrate.summary: Sequential Supersaturated Screening (S3) is a sequential design method for screening many candidate factors with relatively few runs, then optimizing the response using a second-order response surface. It assumes a second-order response with linear, interaction, and quadratic effects, measurement noise, and a batch effect. In Stage 1, it adds two-level runs in rounds, constructs designs by coordinate exchange, and progressively eliminates or commits factors using an importance score and a graduated quantile rule. Its design criterion encourages pairwise column inner products to be positive and balances their spread and magnitude on a scale determined by the Welch lower bound. Simulations and the Borehole benchmark show that it generally selects fewer inactive factors than one-shot cross-validated Lasso while retaining optimization performance, and the paper also gives theoretical bounds for noise-factor commitment and Stage 1 run count.
narrate.key_results: Across the recommended operating ranges in the simulations, S3 had lower Type I error in all eight case-and-size settings: 0.0095 to 0.0715, compared with 0.0910 to 0.3029 for one-shot cross-validated Lasso. Its F1 scores ranged from 0.50 to 0.81, compared with 0.30 to 0.47 for the baseline; this came with higher Type II error in all eight settings. At matched factor counts, S3 had a significant optimization-loss advantage in seven of eight settings, from 0.05 to 0.10 lower loss, with a statistical tie in the weak-signal setting at p = 200. Stage 1 took a mean of 34.8, 58.1, 66.9, and 106.2 runs at p = 40, 80, 120, and 200, respectively, and was faster than the one-shot baseline at each tested size, with median-time ratios from 0.85 to 0.95. On the Borehole benchmark, S3 had lower paired optimization loss than the Welch-design Lasso baseline in 59 of 63 settings, with a mean difference of -5.08; the paper’s Python code is publicly available.

key_equations.name: Observation model
key_equations.explanation: Here y_i is the observed response at setting x_i, f is the second-order response surface, b_d(i) is the effect for the observation’s batch d(i), epsilon_i is measurement error, and sigma and sigma_b are the measurement-noise and batch-effect standard deviations.

key_equations.name: Stage 1 run-count bound

narrate.limitations_stated: The theoretical bound on inactive-factor commitment depends on assumptions about factor survival and commitment at each round; a quantitative link between the elimination schedule and standard high-dimensional regularity conditions remains open. The paper studies two-level screening designs and leaves continuous designs to follow-up work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main simulation study uses a limited set of synthetic signal patterns, while the benchmark is a single evaluable mathematical function rather than a real industrial experiment. The default linear importance scorer is also shown to fail for an interaction-dominated response; alternative scorers are demonstrated in a limited pilot rather than broadly compared.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify the connection between the graduated elimination schedule and standard high-dimensional regularity conditions as an open question. They also leave continuous-design extensions and a budget-aware comparison with controlled sequential bifurcation methods for future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test the method in real industrial experiments and under practical constraints such as restricted factor combinations, run costs, and randomization limits. Broader validation could also compare alternative importance scorers and assess how sequential updates perform when effects or noise levels differ from the assumed model.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for finding which baseline covariates modify which main effects and interactions in a factorial randomized experiment with binary treatment components. It targets linear projection coefficients for the conditional Walsh–Hadamard contrasts, rather than unrestricted conditional effects. The method subtracts a treatment-invariant baseline from an inverse-probability-weighted contrast score, estimates that baseline by cross-fitting, and uses sparse regression with debiasing to estimate modifier coefficients. A multiplier bootstrap supplies simultaneous confidence bands, and a Romano–Wolf step-down procedure selects cells while controlling the familywise error rate (FWER). The authors report that simulations maintained near-nominal coverage and error control across grids of up to 3,150 cells, with accurate cross-fitted baselines improving precision.
narrate.key_results: Across the primary simulations, which included grids from 300 to 3,150 cells, the global-null FWER ranged from 0.045 to 0.059; under sparse signals, simultaneous coverage ranged from 0.940 to 0.953 and strong FWER from 0.046 to 0.057. At a sample size of 1,000, the cross-fitted quadratic baseline produced bands about 1.8% to 1.9% wider than the oracle bands when prognostic variation was present. In the Gaussian simulation settings, multiplier-bootstrap bands were only 0.24% to 0.75% shorter than Bonferroni bands on average, and step-down true-positive rates exceeded Holm’s by 0.3 to 1.0 percentage points. At a sample size of 200, fitting the quadratic baseline without cross-fitting yielded coverage of 0.902, compared with 0.942 for the cross-fitted version.

key_equations.name: Projection target
key_equations.explanation: The coefficient vector θ for contrast S minimizes expected squared error between conditional contrast τ and a linear combination with coefficient vector b of standardized covariates Z; the expectation is over the covariate distribution, and p is the number of features.

narrate.limitations_stated: The target is a projection coefficient tied to the chosen feature dictionary, scaling, and covariate distribution; it is not generally a derivative or a fully nonparametric conditional effect. The theory assumes known randomized assignment, fixed K, and sparse regressions, and its bounded-envelope sufficient conditions may not suit heavier-tailed outcomes or dense coefficients; growing K is not covered.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The finite-sample multiplier calibration uses 1,000 draws in the simulations, but the paper does not quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty in the estimated critical values, especially over repeated step-down sets. The numerical evidence is from simulated settings rather than applied experiments, and the paper does not report runtime or memory benchmarks as the grid grows.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to clustered experiments and observational factorial treatments, where unknown treatment probabilities would require a different orthogonal score. They also identify shared structure across contrasts, nonlinear effect-modification summaries, heavier-tailed settings, and false discovery rate methods as directions for further work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful extension would be to evaluate whether the procedure remains calibrated under constrained or blocked randomization schemes used in practical experiments. Further work could also quantify the computation and multiplier-draw requirements as the grid grows, and validate the approach in real factorial studies.

narrate.summary: The paper compares analysis of variance (ANOVA) models with blocks and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models with quantitative covariates for estimating treatment effects and assessing prediction. It assumes fixed treatment effects and independent, identically distributed Gaussian errors, and develops formal comparisons using the column spaces of the models’ design matrices. The central setting is one where covariate values are constant within a block or within a block-treatment combination. The authors also use simulations of complex soil variability and analyses of piglet and radish experiments to assess model performance. Their main finding is conditional: blocking can be at least as precise under specified conditions, while ANCOVA can improve precision when traditional blocks do not capture complex covariate patterns, without a clear advantage in treatment-test accuracy.
narrate.key_results: Across 500 simulation replicates, ANCOVA had a reported mean square error of 27.26 with no missing covariates, compared with 46.42 to 47.00 for the block models using 3, 4, or 6 blocks. With 60% missing covariate data, ANCOVA’s reported mean square error rose to 40.58 but remained below the block-model values. Treatment-test accuracy was 0.81 to 0.89 for the block models and 0.83 to 0.84 for ANCOVA, so the authors found no marked advantage for ANCOVA on that measure. In the real experiments, some ANCOVA and block-model fits were equivalent; in the radish data, one covariate gave lower residual mean square for plant height under ANCOVA, while the block model had lower residual mean square for tuber weight.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the comparisons under alternative error structures and models that explicitly represent spatial correlation or nonlinear covariate effects. It could also validate the recommendations across more real experiments and assess how covariate-measurement costs and practical randomization constraints affect their usefulness.

narrate.summary: DeltaSelect is a method for affordable, repeated baseline-versus-candidate comparisons of coding agents, rather than for ranking models. It uses repeated public benchmark runs to identify tasks whose single-run results reliably track full-benchmark performance across observed model and reasoning configurations. For each selected task, it maps fail-to-pass (F2P) results onto the benchmark's full-score scale, then scans the fixed task ranking to select tasks within a specified budget. The selected tasks and scoring rules are frozen, and the system must be baselined in its intended harness before comparisons begin. In a case study of revisions to coding-agent skills and instructions, the adopted version cost less than the initial version, while its higher observed score was not statistically established.
narrate.key_results: In the DeepSWE data, only 22 of 113 tasks, or 19.5 percent, had a fifth-percentile one-run correlation of at least 0.50 with the full benchmark score; the median task's fifth-percentile correlation was 0.321. A published-data projection found that nine selected tasks could distinguish two configurations with a projected p-value of 0.0473 at a total cost of USD 113.08, 27.1 times less than the full protocol's recorded cost of USD 3,063.63; this was a projection, not a newly run test. In the target-harness case study, the adopted skills and instructions scored 42.36 percent versus 36.46 percent for the initial version, but the score difference was not statistically significant (p-value 0.326). Recorded cost decreased from USD 4.18 to USD 1.75, a 58.1 percent reduction, and all eight matched task costs were lower for the adopted version.

key_equations.name: Conservative task-ranking statistic
key_equations.explanation: Here q_t is the ranking statistic for task t, Q_0.05 is the fifth-percentile quantile, and r_t^(b) is the correlation for task t in resample b, with 10,000 resamples.

key_equations.name: Per-task score calibration
key_equations.explanation: Here Y_c is the full benchmark score for configuration c, alpha_t and beta_t are the task-specific linear calibration intercept and slope, xbar_tc is the four-run mean F2P for task t and configuration c, and epsilon_tc is the residual error.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the selected subset is intentionally narrow and cannot represent every capability of the full benchmark; repeated development on the same tasks may also specialize a system to those tasks or their verifiers. Their experiments do not establish that this selector is better than random, cheapest-first, or median-correlation selection at matched cost, nor do they isolate the effects of fractional scoring, calibration, or weighting. The evidence uses one DeepSWE snapshot, one model family, and one custom harness, and the case-study uncertainty relies on variance transferred from a different harness.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The development sequence does not use randomized or counterbalanced assignment of versions to runs, so time-related changes in the evaluation environment could be confounded with version changes. Because only a small number of selected tasks are run in each comparison, task-specific events can also have substantial influence on a development decision even when the aggregate score is calibrated.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose matched-cost comparisons with alternative task selectors, nonlinear calibration, equal-weight sensitivity analysis, and methods that account for covariance among related tasks. They also note that repeated runs in the target harness would provide a better estimate of its variability, though at greater cost.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A follow-up study could randomize or counterbalance the order of baseline and candidate runs and repeat both versions to better separate version effects from run and time variation. It could also validate the frozen task sets on held-out tasks and across additional benchmarks, models, and operational harnesses.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for choosing a second-wave experiment to improve a later welfare-maximizing policy choice under constraints. It considers a finite-dimensional parametric model in which policy effects depend on unknown parameters, and assumes that an initial wave of data is already available. The method approximates policy regret with a quadratic function and the information from the experiment with Gaussian estimates, then chooses a design to learn the policy-relevant marginal effects. The authors establish asymptotic optimality under their stated regularity conditions. In a simulation based on the Progresa conditional cash transfer experiment, the tailored second-wave designs substantially reduce expected policy regret compared with repeating the original design.
narrate.key_results: In the Progresa simulations, the proposed design reduced expected regret by 50 to 70 per cent relative to the original Progresa design for samples of 500 or 1,000 observations per wave; gains were smaller but remained positive at 250 observations per wave. For example, at the Boys Primary reference point with 500 observations per wave, expected regret was 2.644 percentage points with the Progresa design, 0.957 with the proposed method, and 0.843 with the oracle design. The paper reports that this reduction in regret corresponds to graduation rates about 1.5 percentage points higher than those attainable using policies estimated from the original Progresa experiment. The proposed designs tended to focus on secondary school and use larger experimental subsidies for smaller treatment groups.

key_equations.name: Quadratic local regret
key_equations.explanation: The local regret r is the sum of the policy adjustment c dotted with the marginal-effect change b and a quadratic curvature term using the constraint-adjusted curvature matrix H̄, with c restricted to the feasible cone G.

key_equations.name: Second-wave design criterion
key_equations.explanation: The optimal second-wave design δ₂* minimizes the expected approximate policy value V of the posterior mean marginal-effect estimate b̂₂, conditional on the first-wave data D₁ and the chosen design δ, among feasible designs Δ.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their asymptotic optimality result is for Bayes regret and that extending it to minimax regret is left for future work. The method assumes a parametric model, locally strongly concave welfare, and two waves that both grow large; the authors note that these conditions rule out some settings, including binary treatment choice with a linear welfare objective.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation is a simulation based on one structural model and historical Progresa data, with local uncertainty centered on four calibrated reference points; it does not establish that the gains carry over to other settings or to parameter values far from those points. The method's design recommendations depend on the structural model and its estimated information, so misspecification could direct the experiment toward the wrong policy margins; the simulations also report that some optimization replications did not converge.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors leave analysis of minimax regret for future work. They also identify use of their asymptotic representation theorem to study efficiency of estimators and tests in adaptive experiments with continuous treatments as a direction for future research.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the procedure prospectively in a field experiment and test its robustness to misspecified structural models and welfare functions. Further work could also develop operational software and examine sequential or multi-wave implementations under practical budget, ethical, and treatment-assignment constraints.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a risk-aware approach to Bayesian optimal experimental design that chooses measurements to improve predictions rather than only estimate model parameters. Its objective combines posterior predictive spread, aggregation across prediction locations, and risk across possible datasets, allowing practitioners to emphasize adverse tails at each stage. The authors construct a differentiable estimator using nested sampling and shared importance weights, then optimize continuous allocation weights over candidate measurement locations. They demonstrate the approach with an analytically tractable linear-Gaussian example and a simulated environmental monitoring problem governed by an advection-diffusion model. In the latter, risk preferences changed sensor allocations, and prediction-focused designs substantially outperformed the parameter-focused baseline on prediction objectives.
narrate.key_results: In the advection-dominated environmental monitoring example, the design used 50 candidate sensors and 20 downstream prediction locations, with 4,000 outer and 4,000 inner samples; the authors also assessed design variability using 30 bootstrap resamples. Risk-aware prediction designs concentrated much of their weight on sensor 26, with some objectives assigning it about 0.7, while the expected-information-gain baseline assigned it essentially zero and instead spread weight across other sensors. Under prediction objectives, the parameter-focused baseline performed about as well as random allocations; conversely, prediction-focused designs performed about as well as random allocations under the parameter-focused objective. When comparing different prediction-focused objectives, using a design optimized for another risk preference incurred gaps of up to 20–25%, while the level-two average-value-at-risk choice interpolated between spatial averaging and a worst-component criterion.

key_equations.explanation: The design objective U is evaluated at allocation vector w; the outer risk operator R aggregates across possible datasets y drawn from p, the middle risk operator R aggregates prediction components under measure mu, and the deviation operator D measures uncertainty in component prediction q_j of parameter theta, with j indexing the Q components.

key_equations.name: Continuous allocation constraint
key_equations.explanation: Each candidate condition k has a nonnegative allocation weight w_k, and the weights across all K candidates sum to one.

key_equations.name: Advection-diffusion application model
key_equations.explanation: The contaminant concentration c changes over time t under velocity u and diffusivity D, with source s at location x depending on uncertain parameter theta.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their design parameterization relies on a Gaussian observation model. They also report poor scaling of the nested importance-weighted estimator when sensor noise is extremely large, beyond approximately 100 candidate locations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstration is centered on one simulated environmental transport problem, with a specified source prior, physics model, and candidate layout, so performance across other systems and real monitoring data remains untested. The optimized design is continuous and is converted to integer measurement counts by a rounding rule rather than by directly solving a constrained integer design problem; rounding could change performance at small budgets.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to sequential optimal experimental design and reducing computational cost by replacing importance sampling with amortized generative models, including models based on normalizing flows. They also identify broader support for larger candidate sets and non-Gaussian likelihoods as goals.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation using field measurements and independently specified transport or source models, to test whether the recommended sensor locations remain effective under model mismatch. Further work could also compare the rounding rule with direct integer-budget optimization under practical siting, access, and per-sensor cost constraints.

narrate.summary: Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED) is a method for choosing experiments when the goal is to distinguish structural families but persistent nuisance uncertainty can make observations hard to interpret. Instead of maximizing expected information gain (EIG), the method seeks the experiment that can support the smallest nonempty set of structural explanations while controlling the chance of excluding the truth. It allows validity to be required at every nuisance state, on average across nuisance states, or in an adverse upper tail of the nuisance distribution. The authors establish that an experiment can score highly on information measures yet provide poor valid structural resolution when the same observation has different meanings across nuisance states. narrate.summary: This paper studies how the purpose of flood monitoring affects where to place a single water-depth sensor. It applies Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) to a simulated flood in metropolitan Detroit, comparing designs that learn model parameters with designs that inform specified flood predictions. The authors use a neural-network surrogate trained on simulations from a six-parameter uncertainty model and evaluate 2,576 candidate locations. They construct expected information gain (EIG) rankings for point, multi-location, regional-average, and regional-maximum predictions, and also examine parameter learning at different observation times. The main finding is that the best location depends on the monitoring objective: point-depth targets favor nearby measurements, while regional targets can favor remote ones.
narrate.key_results: The surrogate was trained using 200 flood-model simulations, and its reported root mean square errors for two displayed field comparisons were of order 10^-2 meters. Rankings were evaluated over 2,576 candidate locations, using a common observation-error standard deviation of 0.05 meters. Point predictions had nearby max-EIG locations, whereas regional-average targets had max-EIG locations outside their target regions; regional maximum-depth targets produced both local and remote maxima depending on the region. The authors report qualitative ranking differences rather than numerical EIG values or a numerical ranking against alternative placement methods; public-data feasibility classes counted 782 high, 1,753 medium, and 41 low locations, while context classes counted 938 high, 1,602 medium, and 36 low locations.

narrate.summary: The paper extends quantile-stratified (QS) sampling to multivariate distributions, with the aim of generating samples that cover density levels more evenly than independent and identically distributed sampling. They report that QS samples have smoother ordered log-density values, while quasi-QS can be computationally costly because it requires a larger base sample.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a framework for estimating microscopic Hamiltonian parameters and planning measurements for the quantum magnet NiPS3. In the simulated comparison, powder-only estimates had the largest errors for most parameters, while adding powder information narrowed posterior distributions for some weakly constrained parameters but did not uniformly lower point-estimation error relative to single-crystal-only measurements. narrate.summary: The paper proposes Target-Weighted Neyman Allocation (TWNA), a design for estimating group average treatment effects (GATEs) when an experiment’s population has different group proportions from the population where results will be used. Its objective is to minimize estimation error weighted by each group’s share in that target population. The design first runs a balanced pilot to estimate outcome variability by group and treatment arm, then allocates the final sample across groups and treatment arms using those estimates and the target shares. It also gives rules for uncertain target shares and a stabilized version for noisy or heavy-tailed pilot data. In simulations and benchmarks using real covariates with simulated outcomes, the design often improves on standard allocation alternatives and approaches the oracle design as pilot estimates become more reliable.
narrate.key_results: In the simulations with a final sample of 5,000 and a pilot of 1,000, TWNA’s relative target-weighted mean squared error was within 0.005 of the oracle in every scenario; in the aligned shift-and-variance scenario it was 0.693, compared with 1.000 for uniform balanced allocation. In the calibrated benchmark using real covariates and simulated outcomes, TWNA scored 0.837, compared with 0.908 for the Hahn–Hirano–Karlan plug-in design and 0.843 for the oracle. On the infant health development program benchmark, TWNA scored 0.884 compared with 1.017 for the Hahn–Hirano–Karlan design and 0.931 for the oracle. Average design regret fell by 93.5% as pilot size increased from 100 to 1,000; in the main simulation interval comparison, the target-weighted mean interval width was 0.304 for TWNA and 0.324 for uniform allocation at a final sample of 5,000 and a pilot of 1,000.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sampling-calibrated stratum-imbalance Gaussian approximation (SIGA-S) and a randomization-calibrated version (SIGA-R) for power and sample-size evaluation in two-arm clinical trials using Pocock–Simon biased-coin minimization. Both procedures replace repeated inner-loop regeneration of treatment assignments with reusable allocation-only simulations. Their construction separates a treatment statistic into a joint-stratum imbalance component and an orthogonal within-stratum component. The sampling-calibrated procedure targets repeated-sampling inference for a marginal treatment effect, while the randomization-calibrated procedure targets the conditional distribution of a prespecified fixed-score randomization test. Simulations show close agreement with the corresponding reference tests while substantially reducing computation.
narrate.key_results: Across 56 practical simulation scenarios, the largest difference from the reference randomization test was 0.42 percentage points for SIGA-S and 0.32 percentage points for SIGA-R. The practical scenarios had mean randomization-to-sampling variance ratios from 1.000 to 1.042; in deliberately strong sensitivity scenarios, the mean ratio reached about 1.19, and SIGA-R tracked the reference test more closely than SIGA-S. For 100,000 analyses, reported SIGA-S runtimes ranged from 0.050 to 2.259 minutes, compared with 113.04 to 2,625.76 minutes for nested rerandomization. In the trial-inspired example, estimated power was 81.48% for unadjusted SIGA-S, 81.44% for unadjusted SIGA-R, and 81.28% for the reference test; total method-specific times were 0.98, 0.85, and 406.36 minutes, respectively.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a policy-aware way to design and analyze online A/B tests of personalized policies. It targets estimation of the average treatment effect while reducing the variance of estimates when the policies select the same actions in some contexts. The method treats randomized assignment between the two policies as a mixture policy, then uses counterfactual weighting to focus estimation on where the policies differ. The authors also derive a traffic allocation that minimizes estimator variance, propose a reward-model training objective, and extend the approach to ranking policies. Theoretical results and simulations show that the method can reduce variance relative to standard difference-in-means testing, especially when policy overlap is substantial.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that their policy-aware inverse propensity estimator has variance no greater than the difference-in-means estimator for any nonzero traffic split, with strict improvement when overlapping actions have residual outcome variance. In a simulated asymmetric policy comparison, the variance-minimizing allocation assigned about 0.81 of traffic to the exploratory policy and reduced variance by about 18% versus an even split. In a heterogeneous simulation, the proposed reward-model training objective reduced variance by about 75% relative to the policy-aware inverse propensity baseline and about 8% relative to the doubly robust estimator; reported mean squared errors were 0.0100, 0.0027, and 0.0025, respectively. The single-action simulations covered action spaces from 10 to 5,000 actions, while the ranking simulation used 100 items and rankings of 25 positions; the baselined ranking estimator reduced variance across the tested policy-divergence range.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an order-of-addition (OofA) approach to prompt engineering: it uses designed experiments to measure how prompt component order and wording affect a large language model (LLM). The demonstration task is to generate two-level fractional factorial designs with maximum resolution and minimum aberration. The authors vary prompt-element order and, in some experiments, wording, then model the probability of a successful design using logistic regression with pairwise-ordering effects. They use fractional OofA designs to study many prompt configurations with fewer tests than a full ordering factorial would require. In confirmation runs, optimized prompts substantially improved success for both tested LLMs on selected design-generation tasks.
narrate.key_results: For the first experiment, the authors tested 48 combinations of order and wording, with 40 repetitions for each of six tasks involving 16-run designs with seven to 12 factors; both factors affected gpt-4.1 success, and the wording of the factor-count and run-count phrase was particularly influential for four tasks. For the 16-run, nine-factor task, an 80-test design with 20 repetitions per test was used instead of the 240-test full design; a follow-up test found 98.3% success for the selected prompt versus 11.7% for the base prompt. For gemini-2.5-flash on the 16-run, seven-factor task, the selected prompts achieved 100% success in confirmation runs, compared with about 35% for the original prompt. The fitted interaction models had McFadden pseudo R-squared values of 0.773 for the gpt-4.1 task and 0.789 for the Gemini task; the paper also reports that newer GPT and Gemini models showed order effects in a smaller five-sequence test.

key_equations.name: Binomial logistic pairwise-ordering model
key_equations.explanation: Y is the number of successful task completions among N_r repetitions, p is the success probability, z_ij codes whether component i comes before component j, w_i codes the version of component i, and beta_0, beta_ij, and gamma_i are the fitted intercept and effects.

key_equations.name: Pairwise-ordering coding
key_equations.explanation: The symbol z_ij is the pairwise-ordering code for components i and j, taking the value 1 when i precedes j and minus 1 otherwise.

key_equations.name: Generalized word length measure
key_equations.explanation: A_k is the generalized word length value for interaction order k, n is the number of design runs, 1_n is a column of n ones, and X_k contains the contrast vectors for the k-factor interactions.

key_equations.name: Fractional ordering-factorial construction
key_equations.explanation: F_{N,q} is an N-run order-of-addition design for q components, X is an N_f-run two-level design for component versions, 1_N and 1_{N_f} are columns of ones of the indicated lengths, and the Kronecker products combine ordering and version settings.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the reduced logistic model with interactions is less interpretable than the main-effects model. They also state that their application is restricted to generating two-level fractional factorial designs and identify additional task types as future applications.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The demonstrations cover selected tasks and a small set of LLMs, so the results do not establish that the same prompt effects will hold for other models, tasks, or engineering settings. The repetitions were API executions with temperature set to zero, and the paper does not establish how stable the optimized prompts are under model updates or other sampling settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing OofA designs and models for nested prompt components, such as phrases within a larger instruction element. They also propose custom optimal OofA designs for logistic pairwise-ordering models and applications to other tasks, including multiple-choice benchmarks and few-shot examples.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test whether the optimized prompts remain effective across model versions, nonzero sampling settings, and independently run replications. It could also compare the method’s cost and predictive performance with alternative prompt-search methods on practical engineering tasks beyond the design-generation examples.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces a fine-tuning method for large language models that aims to improve sequential information gathering without doing extra design optimization at inference time. It trains question-asking policies to maximize expected information gain while also rewarding successful completion of the task. The method estimates information gain using plausible target entities and the model’s predicted likelihoods for possible answers, then uses these rewards in multi-turn policy training. The authors train on the 20 Questions game and evaluate on held-out animal and plant categories and on the medical information-seeking benchmark MediQ. The method improves success on the 20 Questions task, greatly reduces inference time relative to an inference-time design baseline, and shows some transfer to MediQ at the 7-billion-parameter scale.
narrate.key_results: On the 7-billion-parameter model, success increased from 7.6% to 21.0% for animals and from 6.8% to 16.6% for plants; on the 14-billion-parameter model, it increased from 35.0% to 39.2% for animals and from 11.8% to 13.6% for plants. The method outperformed the inference-time Bayesian design baseline in two of the four model-category settings, while the baseline had higher success in the other two. Inference time was approximately the same as for the base model, whereas the inference-time baseline took 25.7 to 36.1 times as long per episode. On MediQ, the 7-billion-parameter model’s accuracy rose from 46.7% to 47.6%, and its voluntary accuracy rose from 50.1% to 51.8%; the reported general language benchmark scores showed no meaningful change after fine-tuning.

key_equations.name: Sequential information-gain criterion
key_equations.explanation: Expected information gain for target θ and design ξ given history h equals the entropy H of outcomes Y predicted from the design and history, minus the expectation E over targets given the history of the entropy of outcomes conditional on the target and design.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report weaker behavioral adaptation for the 14-billion-parameter model and mixed MediQ results at that scale, including slightly lower voluntary accuracy and marginally higher overconfidence. They do not provide a separate limitations section.
narrate.limitations_unstated: Evaluation of the 20 Questions task uses only two held-out categories and averages over five episodes, so results may not represent broader target domains or run-to-run variation. The training game relies on a language-model oracle and the medical evaluation uses a simulated patient, leaving performance with real people, noisy observations, and operational constraints untested.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose separating the effects of the information-gain and outcome rewards, evaluating broader sequential information-gathering benchmarks, and extending the method to reasoning models that generate intermediate reasoning steps.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test other experimental-design objectives and models with noisy or costly outcomes, as well as practical constraints such as limited measurement budgets. Testing sequential deployment with real users or experiments, and validating whether the learned policy remains effective as observations accumulate over time, would clarify its practical transfer.

narrate.summary: The paper compares active-learning designs for identifying building thermal dynamics, with the goal of collecting informative experiments and improving prediction. It studies a deterministic feedforward neural network and a stochastic Gaussian process model. Fourteen acquisition methods are organized into data-space, uncertainty, information-gain, and model-change categories, then used to select control inputs for simulated experiments. The evaluation uses a building energy simulator and compares the resulting models with passive learning based on uniformly random inputs. Active learning usually lowers prediction error, with its advantage most consistent when initial data are scarce and control changes are tightly constrained.
narrate.key_results: Across the reported scenarios, active-learning methods reduce prediction error relative to passive learning in most reported window-and-metric comparisons, but improvement is not universal. The largest reported reduction is 54%: inverse distance weighting with the Gaussian process model lowered the 0–12 hour final error from 5.467°C to 2.503°C in the two-initial-point, tightest-ramp scenario. For the neural network with 10 initial points, query-by-committee reduced the 0–2 hour mean error by 42%, from 5.659°C to 3.297°C. With 10 initial points and the widest ramp constraints, advantages narrowed: the Gaussian process maximum-variance method improved the 0–12 hour final error by less than 1%, and passive learning had the lowest neural-network final error over 0–24 hours.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the study considers a relatively simple system with four model inputs and one output, and does not assess the computational cost of the investigated algorithms. They also note that statistical analysis over repeated trials was not incorporated.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses one simulated BESTEST building case and a limited set of simulated operating scenarios; it does not establish that the relative performance will transfer to other building types or real installations. The reported comparison also does not show repeated-run variability or a broad comparison across alternative passive input-generation strategies.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the study to more complex nonlinear building systems. They also plan to incorporate statistical analysis over repeated trials and measure the computational cost of each acquisition function.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could validate the sampling methods in real buildings and evaluate performance under changing occupancy, disturbances, and equipment constraints. It could also compare sequential or safety-aware acquisition strategies that account for operational objectives as well as prediction error.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces FairBED, a method for designing data acquisition so that the resulting data are useful for prediction but reveal less about sensitive attributes. It formulates Bayesian experimental design (BED) objectives that reward expected information gain (EIG) about a target quantity and penalize EIG about a sensitive attribute, with unconditional and conditional versions. The method is demonstrated both for general experimental design and for active learning (AL), where it selects inputs to label. The authors prove that, under stated assumptions, the conditional objective can ensure demographic parity (DP) for downstream predictions. In simulations and public benchmark datasets, FairBED generally improves fairness measures compared with random acquisition and conventional information-seeking designs, while retaining useful target prediction performance.
narrate.key_results: In the source-location simulation with 10 experiments, the ratio of sensitive-attribute to target EIG was 0.077 (standard error 0.004) for static FairBED, compared with 1.009 (0.034) for random designs and 0.981 (0.007) for standard static BED; for the conditional ratio, the corresponding values were 0.290 (0.009), 1.402 (0.044), and 1.050 (0.007). In active learning with a label budget of 400, the DP ratio at beta 10 was 0.68 (0.06) for FairBED and 0.54 (0.01) for random acquisition on Census, and 0.70 (0.02) and 0.61 (0.01) on Student Graduation; a ratio of 1 is the stated ideal. On CelebA, with a label budget of 300, the DP ratio was 0.83 (0.03) for FairBED and 0.65 (0.09) for random acquisition, while target accuracy was 0.645 (0.013) and 0.693 (0.005), respectively. The authors also report improved fairness-accuracy trade-offs over random acquisition and similar trade-off patterns across several downstream classifier types, but note an exception for the false-positive-rate equalized-odds comparison on CelebA.

key_equations.name: Unconditional FairBED objective
key_equations.explanation: R_u is the unconditional FairBED score, π_d is the design policy, EIG is expected information gain, θ is the target quantity, ϕ is the sensitive attribute, and β weights the sensitive-information penalty.

key_equations.name: Conditional FairBED objective
key_equations.explanation: R_c is the conditional FairBED score, π_d is the design policy, EIG is expected information gain, θ is the target quantity, ϕ is the sensitive attribute, p(θ) is the prior distribution of the target, and β weights the expected conditional sensitive-information penalty.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the conditional fairness objective can be more computationally challenging and requires a joint model for the target and sensitive attributes. Their demographic-parity result requires independent target and sensitive-attribute priors and a downstream predictor that does not use the sensitive attribute; test-time covariates can still affect marginal parity.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The general experimental-design evaluation is limited to a synthetic source-location problem, while the active-learning evaluations use a small set of public datasets and binary sensitive labels. The acquisition strategy depends on the adequacy of the models used to estimate target and sensitive information, and the experiments do not establish how robust its trade-offs are to model misspecification or real-world acquisition constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest exploring FairBED for individual fairness applications, noting that its conditional objective has a connection to individual predictions being independent of the sensitive attribute.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method with multiple sensitive attributes, explicit sampling or cost constraints, and real prospective experiments. It could also assess sequential deployment under changing data distributions and evaluate how robust the acquisition choices are when the sensitive-attribute model is inaccurate.

narrate.summary: The paper examines how to apply Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED) to estimate treatment effects in randomized online experiments. It compares model-free and regression-based adjustments, then studies how to construct adjusted group means and estimate uncertainty. Its design-based analysis covers standard two-group experiments, experiments with multiple treatment groups, and experiments that first sample eligible participants and then assign treatment. The authors derive recommendations for adjustment coefficients and variance estimation, and evaluate them with simulations and operational data from ByteDance. They find that using appropriate adjustments can improve precision, but careless variance estimation can make statistical conclusions unreliable.
narrate.key_results: For regression adjustment, the authors recommend a heteroscedasticity-robust sandwich variance estimate: in their null simulations, its Type I error rates were 4.20%, 3.94%, and 4.64% across three allocations, while ordinary least squares variance estimates gave 2.30%, 3.93%, and 6.82%. In the three-arm experiment comparison, the full-sample covariate mean had empirical power of 68.37%, 80.40%, and 87.11% across three allocation schemes; the corrected pairwise-mean approach had power of 36.26%, 53.32%, and 70.56%, while its uncorrected version had Type I error rates of 18.46%, 13.72%, and 9.48%. In two-stage sampling, using 10,000 sampled participants, the corrected split-sample variance estimate achieved confidence-interval coverage of 95.45%, 95.22%, and 95.03% at sampling probabilities of 0.50, 0.25, and 0.125, respectively; the uncorrected estimate undercovered at 94.82%, 94.62%, and 94.33%. Across five operational experiments, full-sample centering did not reduce variance less than the corrected pairwise approach, and it gave an additional 10% variance reduction in one reported scenario.

key_equations.name: Split-sample adjusted treatment effect
key_equations.explanation: The estimated effect is the adjusted treatment outcome mean minus the adjusted control outcome mean; Ȳ₁ and Ȳ₀ are the group outcome means, b̂₁ and b̂₀ are the group-specific adjustment coefficients, X̄₁ and X̄₀ are the group covariate means, and X̄ is the full-sample covariate mean.

key_equations.name: Group-specific adjustment coefficient
key_equations.explanation: The estimated coefficient for group k is the sample covariance between its outcome Yₖ and covariate Xₖ divided by the sample variance of Xₖ; k indexes control or treatment.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say the five operational experiments are illustrative and that substantial additional variance reduction is not achieved in every online experiment, noting that many experiments include numerous A/A tests. They also describe the multi-arm analysis using a three-arm setup, with larger numbers of treatment arms said to follow analogous logic.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The operational comparisons cover only five anonymized experiments, and the paper does not provide their metric names or enough detail for independent replication of those comparisons. The theoretical results rely on design-based asymptotic conditions and linear covariate adjustments, so the reported guarantees may not directly address small experiments, many covariates, or adjustments selected through more flexible modeling.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the recommended estimators with more varied covariates, allocation constraints, and operational outcomes, and report enough detail for independent validation. It would also be useful to study sequential use of these adjustments and variance corrections in experiments where eligibility or treatment allocation changes over time.

narrate.summary: The paper extends an existing adaptive sampling method to build polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) surrogates for models with multiple quantities of interest (QoIs). Its objective is to improve predictions and estimates of output variability while limiting costly evaluations of the original engineering model. The method scores candidate inputs using a normalized aggregation of local variance contributions across outputs, combined with the distance to the nearest existing sample. The authors test it on a synthetic function, a reinforced concrete beam, and offshore wind turbine examples, comparing it mainly with Latin hypercube sampling (LHS). They report that the new criterion generally improves accuracy, stability, and estimation of second-order statistics, especially when the available sample budget is limited.
narrate.key_results: For the synthetic two-output singularity example, the authors compare results over 100 independent runs and report faster reductions in prediction error, relative variance error, and leave-one-out (LOO) error for the proposed criterion than for LHS. The reinforced concrete beam example has 15 outputs and 8 random inputs; across the plotted run sizes, which extend to 500 samples, the proposed method generally lowers maximum absolute error and improves model stability, while variance-error performance is comparable or better depending on the output and sampling stage. In the wind-excitation case, with two outputs and plotted run sizes extending to 1,000 samples, the method improves control of worst-case error and variance estimation, though mean absolute error for one output is comparable and for the other is slightly higher than LHS. In the multiphysics wind-turbine case, the authors use a pool of 1,000 samples, hold 100 for testing, and use the other 900 as the initial training set and candidate pool; the proposed criterion improves early and intermediate convergence, with performance becoming comparable to the LHS subset around 200 samples before surpassing it for one output’s LOO error. The variance reference in the wind-excitation case is estimated using 100,000 Monte Carlo samples.

key_equations.name: Multi-output polynomial chaos expansion
key_equations.explanation: Y sub r is output r, xi is the standardized input vector, A is the retained set of polynomial indices, alpha is one such index, beta sub r alpha is its coefficient for output r, and Psi sub alpha is the corresponding polynomial basis function.

key_equations.name: Local variance contribution
key_equations.explanation: v sub r is the local variance contribution for output r at input xi, A is the retained polynomial-index set, alpha indexes its nonconstant terms, beta sub r alpha is a PCE coefficient, Psi sub alpha is a basis function, and p sub xi is the probability density of the standardized inputs.

key_equations.name: Multi-output theta sampling criterion
key_equations.explanation: Theta of candidate c is its score, N sub o is the number of outputs, r indexes outputs, v sub r is their local variance contribution, C is the candidate set, S is the set of nearest existing samples, s is the nearest existing sample to c, d is their Euclidean distance, and M is the number of input dimensions; the maxima normalize each output’s contributions over the indicated set.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method depends on a predefined candidate pool, whose construction may be computationally prohibitive in high-dimensional problems and whose quality can limit performance. Repeated surrogate updates can also be costly, particularly when sparse regression and many outputs are involved.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons are mainly against LHS, so the paper does not establish how the criterion performs relative to a broad range of other adaptive or model-based designs. The examples use simulated models and selected engineering cases; results may differ for real experiments, other response structures, or situations where prediction accuracy in low-variance regions is important.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose accounting more explicitly for dependencies among outputs, for example by applying principal component analysis (PCA) before forming the variance-based criterion. They also suggest combining the method with multi-element PCE and other regression-based PCE approaches, and note that sparse solvers designed for vector-valued PCEs may help with computational cost.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the criterion against other adaptive sampling methods and examine how its performance changes with candidate-pool size and construction. It could also evaluate sequential stopping rules and validate the sampling strategy using measured data from physical engineering experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper studies a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with arriving arms (MAB-AA), where new options become available over time and remain available. It designs Upper Confidence Bound for Arriving Arms (UCB-AA), a sequential elimination method intended to optimize reward relative to the best option currently available. The method screens new arrivals against established candidates before allowing survivors into full competition, aiming to avoid spending too many samples on clearly inferior options. Its theoretical analysis bounds regret under conditions controlling how gaps and benchmark improvements evolve, and it also gives a version for an unknown horizon. The authors report that simulations show fewer wasted pulls and a smaller active set, with regret competitive with a growing version of MOSS.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical regret bound is of square-root order in the product of the effective number of arms and the expected number of pulls, with a logarithmic factor, under the stated gap-stability and benchmark-jump conditions. The paper's near-tied-arrival lower bound has square-root order in the number of arriving challengers times the horizon, so the upper bound matches that dependence up to logarithmic factors. Simulations used a horizon of 60,000 and 100 independent runs in each of two scenarios; the figures report averages with 95 percent confidence intervals. UCB-AA reduced wasted pulls and retained fewer active arms than the growing UCB1 and elimination-based baselines, while its dynamic regret was often comparable to Growing MOSS, which was sometimes better.

key_equations.name: Dynamic regret criterion
key_equations.explanation: R_T is cumulative dynamic regret, T is the horizon, t is time, r*(t) is the largest mean reward among the arms A_t available at time t, I_t is the selected arm, and r_i is arm i's mean reward.

key_equations.name: Elimination rule
key_equations.explanation: The candidate arm j is removed when its empirical mean hat r_j plus the phase-p confidence radius b_p is no greater than the largest empirical mean hat r_i minus that radius among reference arms i in set R.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that sublinear regret cannot generally be guaranteed without regularity conditions on arrivals and gap evolution. Their dynamic-regret guarantee relies on stated gap-stability and cumulative-jump-control assumptions, which they describe as sufficient rather than necessary. The fixed-horizon analysis also assumes a known upper bound on the number of arrivals.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The model assumes arrivals are exogenous, arm rewards remain stationary after arrival, and rewards are independent across arms; performance under dependent or changing outcomes is not established here. The round-based screening can delay response to a better arrival, and the evidence for practical performance comes from two synthetic scenarios rather than real experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose incorporating contextual information or arm-level covariates, studying reward drift after an arm arrives, and extending the framework to delayed feedback and operational resource constraints. They also identify using arrival processes calibrated from real application data as a direction for future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method in real sequential experiments and report operational measures such as sample allocation, delay in adopting a superior option, and active-set maintenance costs. Further work could also compare adaptive round schedules and screening thresholds under constrained budgets and varied arrival patterns.

narrate.summary: This paper designs a variance-reduction approach for randomized ranking and recommendation experiments that measure heavy-tailed monetization outcomes. It combines post-stratification by pre-experiment revenue behavior with Controlled Experiments Using Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED) adjustment within each stratum. The stratum estimates are combined using each stratum’s proportion in the full platform population, with strata defined before treatment outcomes are observed. The authors evaluated the method in simulations and in more than 40 operational experiments at ShareChat and Moj. They report substantially lower variance and faster decisions, while cautioning that the approach is not suitable when the main objective is to measure effects on the highest-spending users.
narrate.key_results: Across more than 40 production experiments, each involving more than 1 million users, post-stratification with CUPED reduced variance by 99.3% with winsorization and 99.7% with raw tails, compared with raw GMV. CUPED-adjusted GMV alone reduced variance by 47.62%; the median relative z-score for post-stratification was 1.36, which the paper translates to about 45% less traffic for equivalent confidence, compared with about 17% for CUPED alone. At 10% traffic, the reported minimum detectable effect fell from about 136% of the mean for raw GMV to about 10% for the post-stratified metric, and average time-to-decision fell by about 50%. The production empirical type I error rate for post-stratification was 6.1%; controlled A/A simulations reported 0% false positives for post-stratification across traffic levels from 5% to 50%.

key_equations.name: Population-weighted post-stratified estimator
key_equations.explanation: The estimated post-stratified treatment effect tau-hat-PS is the sum across strata s in the set S of each stratum’s population weight w-s times its CUPED-adjusted treatment-effect estimate tau-hat-s-CUPED; w-s is the full-population count N-s in stratum s divided by the total full-population count N.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors warn that this estimator down-weights the tail and is not appropriate when an experiment specifically targets high-value users. In 1 of more than 40 experiments, it increased variance when the treatment effect was concentrated entirely in the tail and there was stratum-level sample imbalance. They also report a 6.1% empirical type I error rate in production, above the nominal 5%, and recommend longer-horizon confirmation for high-risk launches.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is based primarily on experiments at ShareChat and Moj, so performance in other products, user populations, and monetization settings is not established here. narrate.summary: The paper develops a statistical test for generative surveying, in which model-based personas answer questions about messages using multiple semantically equivalent prompt versions. It focuses on binary responses and on testing whether the average preference differs between two messages. The authors model baseline differences among personas and perturbation effects that can be correlated across personas, then use sign-flips of the message labels across perturbations to construct a permutation test. They show theoretically that common paired tests can have inflated false-positive rates when perturbations create this shared correlation, while the proposed test is valid under their model. Experiments across ten models in two model families support the method and show that both estimated effects and test power depend on model choice and budget allocation.
narrate.key_results: In the motivating example, the sign and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests had null rejection rates above 0.8 at a nominal level of 0.05 in some settings. In the real-data analysis, the sign test was oversized across the tested configurations; at 50 personas, rejection rates reached 0.5 to 0.7 for most models, while the permutation test remained near the nominal level. With 50 personas, 20 perturbations, and 5 replicates, the permutation test reached power of 1.00 for both the Mistral-3 14B and Qwen-3 14B models. Across models, allocating more of a fixed query budget to perturbations rather than replicates generally yielded higher power; the reported 1:10:1 persona-to-perturbation-to-replicate allocation was strongest in the budget simulations. The estimated message effect also differed by model: the Mistral-3 8B and Qwen-3 8B models estimated effects in opposite directions.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus on binary responses for simplicity, although they note that the test can extend to other response summaries when the model is adapted. They also state that results depend on the prompt structure and persona construction used, so conclusions should not be generalized to substantially different designs without validation or re-estimation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical assessment uses one purchase-intent task and ten models from only two model families, so the results do not establish how well the method works across other survey topics or model providers. The test's validity depends on the assumed exchangeability of the two messages under the null and on treating the perturbation-level sign flips as appropriate; the paper does not empirically validate those assumptions for a broad range of practical A/B studies.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the procedure on real human survey outcomes and on varied products, populations, and prompt-generation processes, comparing model-based conclusions with observed preferences. Further work could also study designs with practical restrictions on which perturbations can be used, and assess how the permutation procedure performs when survey budgets permit only a small number of perturbations.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces SimGym, a framework for simulating controlled-versus-treatment storefront tests (A/B tests) of visual interface changes in e-commerce. It uses vision-language model (VLM) agents to shop in live browser sessions and predicts changes in add-to-cart (A2C) behavior. The agents receive buyer personas built from production clickstream data, combining shopping intents with behavioral and value profiles; they use screenshots, webpage structure, session memory, and execution guardrails. The authors compare simulated shifts with observed outcomes from real storefront tests on 50 shops across 16 countries and 11 product categories. They report strong agreement with observed add-to-cart shifts and say the approach can reduce evaluation cycles from weeks to under an hour.
narrate.key_results: With 600 agents per shop, Gemini 3 Flash with visual input achieved 77% directional agreement with observed add-to-cart shifts and a Pearson correlation of 0.55 across the 50 shops; the reported 95% confidence intervals were 66% to 87% and 0.32 to 0.72, respectively. Gemini 3 Flash without visual input achieved 70% agreement and 0.49 correlation, while GPT-OSS without visual input achieved 59% and 0.41. Full personas produced 77% agreement and 0.55 correlation, compared with 44% and 0.02 for shopping intent alone and 51% and -0.14 for product-only inputs; removing session memory reduced results to 42% and 0.00. At 600 agents, runtime per shop was 5.3 minutes for Gemini 3 Flash with vision, 4.5 minutes for its text-only version, and 12.8 minutes for GPT-OSS; the sample-size analysis found that predictive metrics largely plateaued around 300 agents, while the authors used 600 for additional stability.

key_equations.explanation: The alignment rate is the fraction of the 50 shops where the direction of the simulated add-to-cart shift matches the direction of the human-observed shift.

key_equations.explanation: The symbol r is the Pearson correlation, Corr denotes correlation across shops, delta denotes the change, and the simulated and human terms identify the agent-predicted and human-observed add-to-cart shifts.

narrate.limitations_stated: The study evaluates one major e-commerce platform, so generalization beyond that setting remains untested. The reported agents were not post-trained on human traces, and the effect of such training on predictive validity remains to be validated.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses a curated set of 50 theme-change comparisons after excluding cases with other factors that could affect add-to-cart outcomes, so its results may not represent less controlled storefront changes. It reports predictive performance on the skimmers cohort and add-to-cart shifts, leaving performance for other shopper groups and outcomes less established; moreover, the 600-agent run budget may be costly to apply broadly despite the short reported runtime per shop.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose testing the framework beyond one platform and evaluating behavioral targets beyond add-to-cart shifts. They also propose improving agent fidelity through post-training alignment on human traces and using SimGym to screen and prioritize proposed interface changes before merchant-facing experiments.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the approach prospectively across a broader range of interface changes and compare its predictions with subsequent real experiments, including outcomes beyond add-to-cart behavior. It would also be useful to test lower-cost agent budgets and practical constraints such as inventory, pricing, and concurrent promotions, and to examine how sequential simulation results should inform decisions about which variants proceed to live testing.

narrate.summary: The paper designs sequential experiments for settings where an experimenter pays for a study but may have different interests from the regulator deciding whether to approve a treatment. It focuses on comparing two treatments with unknown mean outcomes and a shared Gaussian prior, with clinical trials as the main application. The regulator sets a minimum expected social-welfare requirement, and the experimenter chooses the sampling plan and stopping rule to maximize its own expected payoff subject to that requirement. The construction uses a Neyman allocation across treatment arms and stopping boundaries based on the evolving posterior mean treatment effect. In the paper’s clinical-trial calibration, the design reaches the welfare level of a conventional randomized controlled trial with substantially fewer observations.
narrate.key_results: In the baseline numerical calibration, the adaptive design attained the expected welfare of a fixed-sample randomized controlled trial while using about 48% fewer observations on average, corresponding to an expected stopping time of about 0.52 in the paper’s normalized units. The authors estimate cost savings of nearly USD 6 million and report that about 86% of simulated experiments stopped before the time corresponding to the median clinical-trial sample size of 300 participants. These estimates were based on one million simulated paths and compared the proposed design with a conventional trial at the same welfare level. If the welfare requirement was raised until the adaptive design’s average sample size matched the conventional trial’s, the paper reports a 3.2% welfare gain over the baseline welfare level.

key_equations.name: Experimenter objective under the regulator’s welfare constraint
key_equations.explanation: The design d maximizes the expected experimenter payoff R_B less sampling cost c times stopping time τ, subject to expected regulator welfare R_A being at least V₀; E_d denotes expectation under design d.

key_equations.name: Neyman sampling allocation
key_equations.explanation: The optimal cumulative allocation qₐ at time t is proportional to the outcome standard deviation σₐ in arm a, with the two arm standard deviations σ₀ and σ₁ setting the denominator.

key_equations.name: Stopping rule
key_equations.explanation: The optimal stopping time τ* is the first time t that the posterior mean treatment effect mₜ reaches the upper boundary b⁺(t) or the lower boundary b⁻(t).

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify the shared prior as an important structural assumption and note that it may be harder to justify for genuinely novel treatments than for follow-up treatments or established drug classes. Their stopping-rule analysis also assumes utilities linear in the magnitude of the treatment effect; this implies risk neutrality with respect to that magnitude. The main analysis uses Gaussian priors and known outcome variances, while the authors note that the local asymptotic framework does not capture the effects of estimating those variances.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical findings rely on a calibrated hypothetical clinical-trial setting and simulated experiments, rather than prospective validation in actual trials. The regulator must choose a welfare threshold, but the paper does not establish how institutions can measure and agree on that threshold in practice. The method’s Gaussian prior, constant marginal sampling cost, and restricted treatment comparison may not capture complex trial costs, multiple outcomes, or more than two treatment options.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the stopping and allocation rules in real or historical clinical trials, including whether the reported sample reductions persist under operational constraints such as recruitment limits, interim-review schedules, and safety monitoring. It could also extend the design to non-Gaussian or misspecified priors, multiple treatments and outcomes, and practical procedures for selecting and auditing the regulator’s welfare threshold.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for estimating the frequency response function of a continuous-time, single-input, single-output linear system from nonuniform measurements taken during nonperiodic multisine excitation. It first expresses the output measurements as a least-squares regression in the unknown response values at the excited frequencies. It then chooses a probability distribution for sampling times by maximizing the determinant of the expected information matrix, a criterion that also reduces correlations between frequency components. A greedy procedure converts the distribution-based design into a deterministic sampling sequence, with a time grid used to control spacing between measurements. In simulations on a second-order system, the designed sampling sequence gave lower estimation variance and greater information per measurement than uniform sampling.
narrate.key_results: The authors performed 500 Monte Carlo simulations for a second-order system over a 5-second observation window, comparing the designed sequence with uniform sampling. For a given estimation-accuracy level, the designed sequence required roughly half as many samples as uniform sampling. It also consistently produced higher average information density per measurement and lower summed parameter variance across the tested run sizes. The theoretical analysis establishes that the least-squares estimator is well-posed with probability one when the number of measurements exceeds twice the number of nonzero excitation frequencies, under the stated assumptions.

key_equations.name: D-optimal sampling-density design
key_equations.explanation: The design minimizes the negative natural logarithm of the determinant of the expected information matrix R_0 for sampling density p_T; t is time and T is the observation-window length, while the constraints require a nonnegative density that integrates to one.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that their covariance bound is approximate because it neglects the contribution of rare tail events. They also explain that the grid resolution in the deterministic construction affects how closely the sequence approximates the desired density and how large the minimum spacing between samples is.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison covers one simulated second-order system and compares the proposed sequence only with uniform sampling, so the reported efficiency gain has not been shown across a broad range of systems or design alternatives. The method also relies on a steady-state response, known multisine frequencies, independent sampling times in its analysis, and independent zero-mean noise; performance under departures from these conditions is not evaluated.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the design on real experiments and on systems with different dynamics, noise conditions, and sampling constraints. Further work could also compare it with other sampling-design criteria and investigate sequential updates when measurements arrive during an experiment.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes an adaptive screening method called Probability-of-Hit for finding multiple genetic perturbations whose phenotypic effects exceed a chosen threshold. It models each candidate's response with a probabilistic surrogate and ranks candidates by their estimated probability of exceeding that threshold. The highest-ranked unsampled candidates are selected in batches, tested, and used to update the model for the next round. The authors analyze the method theoretically and evaluate it on simulated functions and five public immunology benchmark datasets. They report improved hit recovery in many comparisons, while noting that performance depends on reliable uncertainty estimates.
narrate.key_results: In synthetic tests with batches of 5 and a 10% hit threshold, Probability-of-Hit reached cumulative hit ratios of 0.88 on the two-dimensional sine dataset, 0.50 on Branin-Hoo, 0.62 on Perturbation-Pathways, and 0.49 on Perturbation-SEM after 10 cycles; the respective random-sampling results were 0.14, 0.15, 0.13, and 0.16. On Perturbation-Pathways, the authors report a four-fold improvement when batch size increased from 2 to 10. On five real benchmark datasets evaluated over 10 cycles with batches of 200, Probability-of-Hit recovered the most hits on three datasets; for Schmidt interleukin-2 it recovered a mean of 575.4 hits, compared with 521.4 for Thompson sampling and 221.2 for random sampling. The authors report an average of 107 more hits than random sampling across the real datasets, while Thompson-Hit performed best on the Zhu SARS-CoV-2 and Zhuang natural-killer datasets.
