narrate.summary: This paper studies how to assign subjects in a two-arm randomized experiment with a binary outcome so that the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test (CMHT) has high power. Subjects are assigned using balanced blocks, which also serve as the test’s strata, and the analysis considers local alternatives to the null hypothesis of equal odds. The authors show that designs are asymptotically optimal when they make the average within-block variation in subjects’ average potential outcome probabilities approach zero. When those probabilities can be ordered, increasingly many blocks meet this condition; when they cannot, pairwise matching (PM) meets it under stated assumptions. Simulations support the theory and suggest that, at smaller sample sizes, using fewer blocks than PM can sometimes yield higher power because of a finite-sample effect.
narrate.key_results: The theorem establishes that the standardized CMHT statistic has an asymptotic normal distribution under the paper’s local alternatives, with a mean determined by the treatment effect and the limiting variance quantity. For one covariate with known ordering, the simulations considered total sample sizes of 48, 96, 192, 288, and 384; at 384 subjects, PM was observed to have the highest power, while at smaller sizes a design with fewer blocks could perform better. For multiple covariates, PM had the highest simulated power among the compared designs, including the cases with 2 and 5 covariates. The simulations used 1,000,000 assignments per cell and a 5 percent test level; for total sample sizes of at least 192, most tested designs had sizes close to the nominal level, while smaller samples showed more size issues and the one-block design was a notable departure.

key_equations.name: Asymptotic CMHT distribution
key_equations.explanation: The standardized CMHT statistic converges in distribution to a normal variable with mean c divided by the square root of eta infinity and variance one, where c describes the local treatment effect and eta infinity is the positive limiting variance quantity.

key_equations.name: Design balance criterion
key_equations.explanation: The criterion requires the quadratic form of v and the allocation covariance matrix for the design with B blocks, divided by twice n, to approach zero as n grows; v contains the subjects’ average potential outcome probabilities.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors study CMHT power but do not study mean squared error for the odds-ratio estimator or confidence-interval coverage. They also analyze offline assignment, where covariates are known before allocation, and identify sequential assignment as a setting for further study.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations use normally distributed covariates and a particular additive treatment-effect model, so they provide limited evidence about other covariate distributions, treatment-effect patterns, or outcome-generating mechanisms. The multivariable blocking procedure deliberately ignores some covariates in the 5-covariate case, and the study does not validate the recommendation using real experiments or report practical matching runtimes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying mean squared error and confidence-interval coverage for odds-ratio inference. They also propose examining sequential experiments in which subjects arrive one at a time and covariates are not all known before assignment.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare these designs under outcome-model misspecification, non-normal covariates, and practical allocation constraints such as limited block sizes or unavailable matches. Testing the recommendations in real experiments and reporting computational time for pairwise matching would help establish their operational value.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a method for constructing exact experimental designs under the determinant-maximizing D-optimality criterion. It targets regression problems with a moderate number of model parameters, a very large set of candidate points, and a run size close to the number of parameters. The method first solves the continuous relaxation using column generation, pruning candidate points that cannot be in the optimal support, and solves the smaller subproblems with a semidefinite programming solver. It then applies local exchanges among the identified support points to form an integer design. The authors report strong computational gains and prove that restricting the local search preserves its stated worst-case approximation bound, although the resulting heuristic is not a globally exact optimization method.
narrate.key_results: For continuous support identification on synthetic datasets with up to 10 million candidate points and model dimensions up to 50, the proposed method was reported to be tens to hundreds of times faster than the Frank–Wolfe (FW) comparator and generally achieved smaller duality gaps. On medium-sized synthetic problems with up to 500 candidate points and dimension 50, the full method produced objective values equal to or better than those from the Boscia exact solver in under 30 seconds; Boscia often did not reach optimality within the 1,800-second limit. On synthetic datasets with 100,000 and 1 million candidates, support identification followed by local search reduced runtime by as much as two orders of magnitude compared with local search over the full candidate set. In the comparison at a run size of twice the model dimension, IBOSS was faster, but its reported optimality gaps were roughly one order of magnitude larger than those of the proposed method.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The theoretical and computational results rely on the specified regression-vector information model and do not test how robust the designs are when that model is misspecified. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to A-optimal experimental design. They identify the need for a dedicated implementation and numerical comparisons, in part because the A-optimal formulation requires additional optimization structure and suitable benchmarks.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method in real prospective experiments and measure whether the selected designs improve parameter estimation under realistic noise and model misspecification. narrate.summary: This paper compares cross-validation with other model-selection approaches for analyzing small designed experiments. It examines prediction in response surface designs and active-factor identification in screening and supersaturated designs. The authors use simulations to compare regression models selected with five-fold cross-validation or leave-one-out cross-validation, the little bootstrap, lasso methods, and random forests. For prediction, the simulations include full and reduced second-order surfaces and more complex sixth-order surfaces; for screening, they include main effects and interactions. Overall, leave-one-out cross-validation for regression is often competitive for both prediction and screening, while the performance of other cross-validation approaches is less consistent.
narrate.key_results: For response surface analysis, the authors simulated 500 repetitions for each analysis method and design, assessing prediction on 1,000 new points. Regression selected by five-fold or leave-one-out cross-validation had broadly similar prediction performance to the little bootstrap, with leave-one-out cross-validation sometimes showing less variability; the little bootstrap provided no clear predictive advantage. For screening with 20 runs and 7 factors, 250 response vectors were evaluated per scenario: regression with leave-one-out cross-validation offered the best overall balance of power and false-positive control, although it failed for the MEPI design. In supersaturated screening, using designs with 12 runs and 26 factors, 14 runs and 24 factors, or 18 runs and 22 factors, regression with leave-one-out cross-validation and Gauss-Lasso were identified as strong choices; lasso with five-fold cross-validation had the lowest power, while lasso with leave-one-out cross-validation had the highest power but also the highest type 1 error. For sixth-order response surfaces, the reported average selected regression model sizes at 16 runs were 3.3 terms for the little bootstrap, 2.4 for five-fold cross-validation, and 2.6 for leave-one-out cross-validation; at 52 runs they were 7.6, 3.4, and 5.4 terms, respectively.

narrate.summary: This paper designs methods for reinforcement learning from human feedback in general Markov decision processes with linear rewards and trajectory-level preference comparisons. The methods assume a Bradley–Terry preference model and access to a probably approximately correct reinforcement learning oracle. The authors use randomized reward-parameter sampling to choose policies, then estimate the reward from preference labels. Their main design contribution collects candidate trajectory pairs in batches and uses greedy D-optimal design to select informative comparisons from each batch. The theoretical results provide regret and final-policy guarantees, while experiments report competitive performance and substantially fewer queries for the design-based method than for its non-design counterpart.
narrate.key_results: The regret guarantee for the online randomized method scales as the square root of the number of rounds, with a factor depending on the preference-model sensitivity, feature dimension, and logarithmic terms; the lazy design variant adds a factor depending on its threshold parameter. The preference-free exploration method guarantees an output-policy suboptimality that decreases with the square root of the number of rounds, and the paper states that an epsilon-optimal policy requires a number of iterations proportional, up to logarithmic terms, to kappa times the feature dimension cubed divided by epsilon squared. The lazy design method retains the stated regret guarantee while limiting design-matrix updates to a logarithmic number and can parallelize preference queries within batches. In Isaac Cartpole experiments, the design-based lazy method reaches similar regret to the online randomized method while using considerably fewer preference queries; the paper does not give a precise query-reduction number in the text. In the preference-free Cartpole experiment, the authors report at most 150 binary preference queries for their method, compared with 4,915,200 ground-truth reward queries for the reward-based baseline.

narrate.summary: This paper develops block designs for order-of-addition (OofA) experiments, where the response may depend on the sequence in which components are added and experimental units may differ by group or batch. The designs use position-based models and a word length pattern (WLP) to assess aliasing among position effects and confounding between position and block effects. The construction method assembles Latin squares (LSs) and component orthogonal arrays (COAs), then searches by exchanging squares or rows to improve the WLP. The paper compares the resulting designs with full block designs using correlation plots, a simulated pharmaceutical example, and simulation studies. The authors find that the designs can substantially reduce runs per block while retaining broadly comparable power and type I error rates in the simulated settings.
narrate.key_results: For five components and three blocks, the design with 12 runs per block reduces block size by 90% relative to the full design with 120 runs per block. With six active position effects, its power is 0.846 versus 0.894 for the full design, and its type I error rate is 0.103 versus 0.088. For five components and two blocks, the design with 25 runs per block reduces block size by 79%; with six active position effects, power is 0.840 versus 0.878 and the type I error rate is 0.100 versus 0.086. In the simulated five-drug example, the blocked design identified the two optimal drug orders from the assumed true model, whereas the analysis that ignored batch effects did not; the paper also reports that the simulated designs for eight components retained high power and low type I error rates.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a method for allocating degrees of freedom (df) in experimental designs with multiple randomization stages, blocking, fractional factorials, missing observations, or unequal replication. It applies to linear mixed models with fixed and random effects and aims to assign exact integer degrees of freedom to each effect and stratum. The method constructs projectors for the randomization strata, intersects their spaces with the contrast spaces for effects, and counts the dimensions of those intersections. It also proposes measures of retained information, lost degrees of freedom, and variance inflation to help compare or plan designs. The paper reports that the method can improve inference and design efficiency, while requiring substantially less computation than a bootstrap approximation in its benchmark.
narrate.key_results: In a split-plot simulation, the method’s empirical type I error was 0.040 in the balanced case and 0.051 with 20% of sub-plots missing, compared with 0.529 and 0.466 for the naive analysis. In a nested animal simulation, the corresponding rates were 2.7% and 7.7% for the method, versus 0.3% and 1.0% for naive one-way analysis. In a comparison of two 16-run fractional factorial designs, the information-retention-optimized design reduced reported lost degrees of freedom from 5 to 2; with the exact method, power for the two active effects increased from 0.42 and 0.41 to 0.61 and 0.60, and mean confidence-interval width decreased from 1.87 to 1.47. At 100,000 observations, the projector-rank calculation took 0.0073 seconds, compared with 0.648 seconds for a 100-draw parametric bootstrap, an 89-fold speed-up.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their design-metadata screening diagnostics do not replace exact computation when a full degrees-of-freedom table is needed. They also describe the simulation studies as demonstrations of structural mechanisms rather than stand-alone evidence.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation covers a small set of simulated design settings and one 16-run design-selection comparison, so it does not establish performance across the full range of models and layouts claimed by the general framework. The method’s exact allocations rely on a correctly specified linear mixed model and the required stratum-projector structure; the paper does not empirically assess sensitivity to model misspecification or to designs whose randomization structures do not meet those conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose integrating the method into statistical software as an analytic alternative to numerical degrees-of-freedom approximations. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the method on real industrial or quality-engineering experiments, where missingness, process constraints, and departures from the assumed model can be assessed directly. Broader comparisons across design families and established approximation methods would also clarify when the exact allocations improve practical error control and power.

narrate.summary: The paper develops structured optimal experimental design (OED) methods for linear Bayesian inverse problems, aiming to maximize expected information gain (EIG), a measure equivalent here to D-optimality. Its central problem is to select groups of design variables together, rather than selecting individual matrix columns independently. The authors reshape the weighted forward model into a tensor and propose three selection strategies: independent selection by mode, sequential selection by mode, and iterative selection by mode. They also introduce a randomized sketch-first version that reduces the matrix size and can avoid forming the full matrix or using the adjoint forward operator. Tests on four application examples find that the methods often deliver high-information designs with substantially lower computational cost than the greedy comparisons.
narrate.key_results: Across the four application examples, the proposed designs exceeded the EIG of sampled random designs; the seismic and X-ray comparisons each included 5,000 random configurations, while flow reconstruction included 2,000. In the time-dependent example, selections of 5 sensors performed better than 96.13% of all possible designs, and selections of 22 sensors performed better than 99.7%; iterative selection converged in 2 iterations in both cases. In seismic tomography, using 10 of 32 sources and 10 of 45 receivers increased relative reconstruction error from 9.4% with all data to 11.5%, while using about 7% of all source-receiver pairs. The paper reports speedups of up to 50 times over its greedy approaches; for example, on the seismic case, deterministic GKS-based independent selection took 0.86349 seconds compared with 18.4519 seconds for the greedy version. In flow reconstruction, the reported EIG values were 95.8917 for independent selection, 97.7939 for sequential selection, and 99.8607 for iterative selection; all exceeded the sampled random designs.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a gradient-free approach to sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED), choosing each next experiment to maximize expected information gain (EIG) about unknown model parameters. It combines ensemble Kalman inversion (EKI) to optimize designs with affine-invariant Langevin dynamics (ALDI) to sample updated parameter distributions. To avoid expensive nested Monte Carlo calculations, it estimates the EIG using Gaussian approximations that provide lower and upper bounds, with a Laplace approximation available to improve the lower bound. The method is tested on linear and mildly nonlinear models and on an inverse problem involving a partial differential equation (PDE). The experiments show that design optimization increases estimated information and that the bounds generally improve as the models become more nearly linear or the approximations become more accurate.
narrate.key_results: For the linear Gaussian example, the authors report that the KL divergence between the true distributions and their Gaussian approximations decreases with sample size; the plotted behavior is described as a rate of order J to the power minus one-half, while a theoretical result gives an L2 convergence rate of order J to the power minus one. The linear design optimization used 100,000 joint samples and was compared with an optimum computed using a high-fidelity double-loop Monte Carlo calculation with 10,000,000 samples; the reported design and observation errors decreased as EKI progressed. In the near-linear example, the Gaussian bounds approached the linear-model bounds as nonlinearity decreased, and the Laplace approximation gave a tighter lower bound, at the cost of solving an optimization problem for each observation. In the heat-equation example, the method used 1,000 samples, three EKI particles, and 15 sequential steps; the authors report increasingly informative selected designs, including for a setting with eight parameters and three observations.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that Gaussian approximations can be less accurate for nonlinear examples, while the Laplace approximation is more computationally expensive because it requires an optimization for each observation. narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical validation uses simulated examples, and the PDE demonstration is limited to a one-dimensional heat equation with at most eight parameters and three observations; performance on real experiments or broader application domains is not established. The examples also assume additive Gaussian noise and begin with a Gaussian prior, and the paper does not demonstrate how the method handles practical design constraints or substantially larger EKI ensembles.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose improving the EIG bounds with more flexible and adaptive approximations, including Gaussian mixtures for nonlinear or multimodal settings. They also propose extending the framework to account for model misspecification and non-Gaussian noise.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on real experiments and compare its design quality and total computational cost with established sequential design methods under the same conditions. It could also incorporate practical constraints on allowable designs and evaluate how reliable the sequential updates remain when the posterior is strongly multimodal or the forward model is misspecified.

narrate.summary: This paper extends a model-robust QB criterion to two-level screening designs without requiring factors to be level-balanced or pairs of factors to be orthogonal. It considers first-order and second-order models, with design quality depending on prior beliefs about which main effects and interactions are active. The authors summarize aliasing using generalized word counts and derive criterion weights from the prior probabilities. They also propose a coordinate-exchange algorithm that repeatedly changes individual design entries to reduce the criterion, using multiple random starts. Examples show that the preferred design can change with the priors, allowing trade-offs between level-balance, pairwise orthogonality, and aliasing among higher-order effects.
narrate.key_results: For 12 runs and 14 factors, the paper reports that the E(s²)-optimal design is preferred when the main-effect prior is at most 0.2, another design is preferred for priors from 0.2 to 0.5, and a third is preferred at 0.5 or higher. For saturated designs with 10 runs and 9 factors, the exchange algorithm's reported A_s efficiencies range from 0.659 to 0.800 across the five prior ranges, compared with 0.593 to 0.741 for the conference-matrix construction. For the second-order example with 16 runs and 6 factors, one design had no non-estimable three-factor projections, while another had higher reported A_s efficiencies than the first for several larger projections; the comparisons also show that which design is preferred depends on the prior and the model size of interest. These are numerical examples rather than a broad benchmark, and the paper does not report a single overall efficiency gain.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an improved rank-based test and sample-size procedures for comparing treatments in a randomized complete block design (RCBD), where blocks account for differences among experimental units. The approach transforms the Friedman rank statistic and compares it with an approximate F distribution, with numerator degrees of freedom matching those of the conventional analysis of variance (ANOVA) test. For power and sample-size planning under treatment location shifts, the authors also develop approximate noncentral F distributions and derive calculations for uniform, normal, Laplace, and exponential populations. The proposed test generally controls Type I error better than the existing approximations examined. For power planning, the proposed noncentral F approach is more accurate in the studied scenarios than the noncentral chi-square approach, especially when the number of blocks is small or moderate.
narrate.key_results: The authors compared Type I error rates using exact critical values for 53 combinations with 3 to 5 treatments and 3 to 8 blocks, and simulation with 100,000 iterations for 36 combinations with 3 to 5 treatments and 5, 10, 15, or 20 blocks. Across these comparisons, the proposed test generally performed favorably against the Friedman chi-square approximation and two existing F approximations. In the power study, the largest reported difference between estimated and simulated power for the noncentral chi-square method was 0.6916, compared with 0.0111 for the proposed noncentral F approach in the corresponding exponential-distribution case. In the cotton-fiber example with 5 treatment levels and 3 blocks, the Friedman test had a p-value of 0.0663, while the proposed transformed test had a p-value of 0.0357. In the same example, the proposed power procedure estimated that 4 to 6 blocks were needed for 0.90 power across the four studied distributions.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential design method for high-dimensional Bayesian inverse problems, with the aim of choosing experiments that maximize expected information gain. At each stage, it selects an experiment by maximizing a derivative-based upper bound on the information expected from the next observation. The method combines likelihood-informed parameter reduction with conditional measure transport maps, which support scalable posterior approximation and inference after data arrive. The authors also give a covariance-based bound for additive Gaussian observation noise and add periodic restarts to improve posterior approximations. In two simulated partial differential equation applications, the selected designs generally performed better than randomly chosen designs when assessed using nested Monte Carlo estimates.
narrate.key_results: In the diffusivity-field example, the unknown parameter had 4,225 coefficients and the method selected sensors from 121 candidates over 8 stages; the reduced-order model used to construct transport maps was approximately 40 times faster than the full model, with relative L2 error of approximately 0.003. In the photoacoustic imaging example, the parameter had 3,969 coefficients, designs combined 2 illumination choices with 50 sensor candidates, and the study used 5 stages; its reduced-order model was approximately 130 times faster than solving the coupled equations, with relative L2 error of approximately 0.01. For the first example, designs maximizing either proposed bound had comparable nested Monte Carlo performance and usually outperformed 50 randomly selected designs; the covariance bound was consistently tighter than the information-based bound in the reported comparison. In the second example, the bound-selected designs consistently outperformed 50 random designs in the reported nested Monte Carlo comparisons. Posterior effective sample-size-per-sample values varied from 0.133 to 0.898 in the first example and from 0.153 to 0.996 across the two simulated cases in the second example.

narrate.summary: This paper develops sequential adaptive designs for estimating the average treatment effect in a finite population. Its noncontextual design modifies ClipOGD, an existing adaptive allocation method, to use a decreasing learning rate and exploit strong convexity of the variance objective. It also introduces MGATE, which uses pre-treatment covariates to adapt assignments for a predefined collection of possibly overlapping groups. Both methods seek to reduce Neyman regret, the gap in estimator variance relative to the best fixed-probability design chosen with hindsight. The theoretical analysis gives near-logarithmic regret for the noncontextual method and a square-root-in-trial-size regret guarantee for the multigroup method, with empirical comparisons generally favoring the proposed designs over the original ClipOGD.
narrate.key_results: Under the paper’s stronger bounded-outcome and lower-bound assumptions, ClipOGDSC has an anytime expected regret bound of order h(T) to the fifth power times log T, plus a term independent of T; choosing h to grow sufficiently slowly gives the stated near-logarithmic rate. MGATE has an anytime multigroup regret bound of order the square root of the number of groups times h(T) to the fifth power times T, yielding the stated square-root-in-T rate up to slowly growing factors. The authors also establish asymptotically valid conservative Chebyshev confidence intervals for clipped designs satisfying their conditions. In experiments, they use 10,000 simulated assignment paths; at 50,000 rounds on synthetic data and about 15,000 rounds on microfinance data, ClipOGDSC’s regret falls while ClipOGD0’s generally stays higher or increases, and MGATE has the lowest group-conditional regret in the reported microfinance comparison. The contextual groups are constructed using outcome information that would not be observable in a real experiment, so those results illustrate the method rather than demonstrate deployable covariate-based grouping.

narrate.limitations_stated: The near-logarithmic noncontextual guarantee requires a stronger outcome assumption than the earlier ClipOGD result, including bounded outcomes and a positive lower bound on outcome second moments. The authors note that choosing the clipping function is nontrivial: slower growth can make its inverse large and lead to slow convergence, especially when the outcome bounds are poorly conditioned. They prove conservative Chebyshev confidence intervals but leave Wald-type intervals for future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The contextual experiments define groups using a score computed from both potential outcomes, which would not be available when assigning treatment in an actual experiment; thus the reported contextual advantage does not validate performance with practical, pre-treatment covariates. The multigroup bound also depends on the number of predefined groups and the clipping schedule, while the paper’s empirical comparisons do not establish performance across a broad range of operational constraints or group definitions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring adaptive designs beyond the sequential finite-population setting, including multigroup guarantees, and extending the work to other experimental designs and further reductions in regret. They also identify exploration of well-conditioning in Neyman regret and proof of Wald-type confidence intervals as open directions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate MGATE using groups defined only by covariates available before treatment assignment, including groups that overlap in real operational data. Further work could also assess the methods under practical assignment constraints and validate regret and confidence interval behavior in prospectively run experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes an active-learning procedure for expensive computer experiments, using a Gaussian process surrogate for both prediction and optimization. Its initial design is a maximum one-factor-at-a-time design, which varies one input at a time along several paths to help identify influential variables with relatively few runs. The method then uses a multiplicative inverse multiquadric kernel, intended to improve low-dimensional projections during sequential sampling. The authors use the Active Learning MacKay criterion for emulation and expected improvement for optimization. Simulations and a vapor-phase infiltration calibration application show that the combined approach can improve performance over the compared space-filling and Gaussian-kernel approaches, especially when some inputs are inactive.
narrate.key_results: In the emulation study, the authors compared the proposed procedure with maximum projection designs and Gaussian-kernel models on six test functions, generally using a 44-run initial design and sampling sequentially up to 100 total runs; results were averaged over 10 runs. The proposed procedure outperformed the compared active-learning approach on all but the piston simulation function, where all procedures were very accurate, and it improved on the 100-point batch-design benchmark across the reported examples. For optimization, the MOFAT design used 4(d + 1) initial runs, compared with maximum projection designs using either 4(d + 1) or 10d runs, and the proposed design and kernel achieved substantially better optimality gaps on the Ackley, Levy, and Rastrigin examples. In the vapor-phase infiltration calibration, the proposed method reached a minimum root mean squared error of approximately 700, below the approximately 800 reported for the earlier method, and found a good setting in fewer than 40 evaluations of the PDE model.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the procedure works best for problems with a moderate number of input dimensions. They also note that MOFAT has somewhat poorer projections than conventional space-filling initial designs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The approach assumes deterministic, error-free evaluations and uses a particular stationary Gaussian-process setup, so noisy experiments or strongly nonstationary responses may require adaptation. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying screening designs and the MIM kernel for variable selection in high-dimensional problems. narrate.summary: The paper designs a sequential Bayesian optimization method for minimizing an expensive black-box objective over conditional search spaces, where different configurations can have different active parameters. Its method, AttnBO, encodes each parameter’s identity, value, index, and parent identity, then uses self-attention and pooling to map configurations into a shared latent space. A single Gaussian process models responses across the different subspaces, allowing observations from one subspace to inform predictions in others. The method selects candidates using an acquisition score and can propose batches of candidates. Across simulations, machine-learning configuration tasks, and benchmark tasks, the authors report improved optimization performance and sample efficiency, alongside some additional computation for model fitting.
narrate.key_results: On the simulated conditional search problem, AttnBO performed best among the compared methods. In a direct comparison with separate Gaussian process models, AttnBO reached the same reported performance with 100 observations that the separate models needed 200 observations to reach. On the three machine-learning search tasks evaluated across six OpenML datasets, the paper reports that AttnBO achieved the best performance on all three tasks. For 100 iterations on the simulation task, AttnBO took 17.05 minutes, compared with 11.96 minutes for Bandits-BO and 12.73 minutes for Add-tree; on the hyperparameter optimization benchmark, warm-started AttnBO was reported as competitive with state-of-the-art transfer-learning methods.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that training the deep encoder makes AttnBO somewhat more computationally expensive than the compared methods. narrate.limitations_unstated: The method assumes that conditional configurations can be represented using a tree structure or a combination of trees, and its transfer of information depends on the learned embeddings capturing meaningful relationships between parameter identities and values. narrate.summary: This paper develops non-myopic Bayesian optimization (BO) methods for finite-budget sequential experimental design (SED) in multi-objective optimization (MOO). The goal is to find a high-quality Pareto front when evaluating each candidate is expensive. The authors use hypervolume improvement (HVI) as a scalar reward, because its successive improvements add up and it reflects Pareto-front quality. They construct nested and joint lookahead methods, plus a faster batch-based method, using Gaussian process models of the objectives. Across the reported benchmarks, the non-myopic methods generally achieved higher hypervolume than the myopic comparison methods, though they required more computation.
narrate.key_results: The authors report that their non-myopic methods outperformed the myopic expected hypervolume improvement and joint entropy search baselines on all six real-world benchmark problems in the main comparison. Experiments used 15 runs per method, five randomly generated initial points, and 65 optimization iterations. In the reinforced concrete beam benchmark, mean runtime per iteration was 1 second for expected hypervolume improvement, 7 seconds for the batch method with a horizon of 4, 52 seconds for the joint method with a horizon of 4, and 560 seconds for the nested method with a horizon of 2; the corresponding reported standard deviations were 0, 4, 19, and 58 seconds. The authors also report that longer horizons often slightly reduced performance, and that the HVI-based batch method generally performed better than its information-gain-based variants.

They also report that the nested method is very time-consuming and that longer horizons can worsen performance as predictive uncertainty accumulates.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The comparisons use specified engineering benchmark functions and synthetic test problems, rather than reported evaluations in physical laboratory experiments, so the results do not establish performance under real experimental noise or operational constraints. The approach also relies on independent Gaussian process models and a hypervolume reference point, so its performance may change with dependent objectives, model misspecification, or a different reference point.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating how tight the lower bounds are and developing a multi-step expected HVI approach analogous to multi-step expected improvement.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the methods in real laboratory or production experiments and assess robustness to noisy, correlated objectives and practical evaluation constraints. narrate.summary: This paper presents a vision and mathematical framework for collaborative black-box optimization, in which multiple agents seek good designs for their own unknown response functions. It focuses on Bayesian optimization and the challenges of allocating experiments, handling differences between agents, and protecting privacy. It organizes possible approaches into three frameworks: centrally coordinated decisions, local decisions informed by shared information, and collaboration that improves agents’ predictive models. The frameworks include consensus over candidate designs, sharing near-optimal design information, and jointly learning model information. The paper is conceptual and reviews methods and open questions rather than reporting a new empirical comparison.
narrate.key_results: The paper organizes federated Bayesian optimization into three frameworks: global decisions, conditioned local decisions, and predictive model improvement. It describes consensus as a way to give agents individualized next designs by combining their candidate designs, rather than having every agent run the same experiment. For local decisions, it discusses constrained Gaussian-process methods that filter shared designs, and reports that the cited approach provides sublinear regret guarantees despite differences between agents. The paper presents no experimental measurements or numerical comparisons of efficiency, run size, or prediction accuracy.

narrate.limitations_stated: The author identifies unresolved issues with privacy, differences in functions and resources, and the theory of consensus methods. The paper also notes that rejection sampling with shared designs can scale poorly, that shared random features impose restrictions, and that a practical collaborative example is still needed.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The frameworks are not evaluated against one another on simulated or real experiments, so their practical trade-offs for quality engineers remain unclear. The presentation also assumes a scalar response and focuses on Bayesian optimization, leaving the treatment of multiple quality characteristics, hard process constraints, and costly or unequal experiments unspecified.
narrate.future_work_stated: The author calls for a practical example in which agents collaborate to improve decisions while preserving privacy and intellectual property. The paper also highlights open research questions about privacy-performance trade-offs, heterogeneity, initialization, and when collaboration should stop.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to benchmark the three frameworks on real manufacturing or process-development studies, including constraints, unequal experiment costs, and different agent capabilities. Further work could also test whether the methods support asynchronous collaboration and multiple response objectives in sequential use.

narrate.summary: The paper examines what difference-in-means estimates measure in randomized online experiments when each unit has repeated outcomes after exposure. It compares metrics that accumulate all post-exposure data, metrics that use a fixed post-exposure window, and metrics that accumulate data only up to that window. The authors derive how each metric’s estimand depends on the treatment-effect curve, exposure timing, analysis time, and window length. They also derive conditions under which the power of a test using a cumulative metric can fall as more observations are collected. Their main finding is that no metric type is best for every purpose: cumulative metrics can give earlier signals, while windowed metrics target a more stable and interpretable effect.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical results show that the cumulative metric’s estimand can change with analysis time and the exposure-time distribution, while the windowed metric targets the cumulative treatment effect at the end of its prespecified window. The authors illustrate power behavior with Monte Carlo simulations using 700 units per replication, 10,000 replications for each data-generating process, a maximum experiment length of 21 days, and a 10% false positive rate. With rapidly decaying effects and exposure concentrated early, cumulative-metric power declines as the experiment proceeds; the cumulative-windowed metric declines less, while the windowed metric reports only after its window has elapsed. With effects peaking later and exposure increasing over time, the windowed metric has higher power than the cumulative metrics in the reported example, and the cumulative-windowed and windowed results have not yet converged by the end of the experiment.

narrate.summary: This paper develops exact designs for order-of-addition (OofA) experiments using a transition-effect (TE) model, in which the response depends on which component directly follows another. The designs target both D-optimality for parameter estimation and I-optimality for prediction, including settings in which components are assigned to ordered blocks. The authors derive moment-matrix results and use simulated annealing, a greedy adjacent-swap method, and a greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP) to search for designs without enumerating every possible order. In numerical comparisons for 9 to 11 components, GRASP generally produced the highest relative efficiencies among the tested search methods. In a scheduling benchmark example, the TE models ranked the lowest-cost order better on average than the pairwise order model.
narrate.key_results: For unconstrained designs with 9, 10, or 11 components and 400, 500, or 600 runs, GRASP had the highest median relative D-optimal and I-optimal efficiencies among the three methods in every reported case. For 9 components and 600 runs, its relative efficiencies were 0.9919 for D-optimality and 0.9841 for I-optimality; for 11 components and 600 runs, they were 0.9707 and 0.9517, respectively. Under block constraints, reported relative efficiencies sometimes exceeded 1, consistent with the authors’ finding that the full feasible design is not necessarily optimal under those constraints; GRASP had the highest I-optimal efficiency in all but two tested cases. In the 11-component scheduling benchmark, average ranks for the estimated best order were 8.50 to 18.58 for the TE models and 45.58 to 56.73 for the pairwise order model across the reported design methods and run sizes.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a design method for randomized controlled trials that aims to estimate the average treatment effect while balancing observed covariates and retaining robustness to unobserved factors. It formulates this goal as distributional discrepancy minimization (DDM), which optimizes the covariance of covariate-weighted randomized assignments and permits unequal treatment probabilities. The authors construct a multiplicative weights update (MWU) algorithm using a randomized-walk oracle, and use it to create a trial design. They prove that finding near-optimal solutions to DDM is computationally hard, while their algorithm improves on the Gram-Schmidt walk (GSW) approach for unequal probabilities in its theoretical guarantee. In simulations and analyses of a public dataset, the MWU design often had lower discrepancy and lower treatment-effect estimation error than the compared designs.
narrate.key_results: The MWU design achieved the lowest reported discrepancy across the tested assignment probabilities in experiments with random matrices and the LaLonde control datasets. For simulated linear or nearly linear outcome-covariate relationships, the best mean squared error from other designs was at least 2.61 times that of MWU with design parameter 0.5 on average, and at least 3.00 times as large for assignment probabilities from 0.25 to 0.85. For quadratic outcomes, rerandomization had the lowest error, while MWU with design parameter 0.9 had error no more than 1.49 times as large. In a nonuniform-probability comparison with group probabilities 0.1 and 0.5, the reported discrepancy objectives were 0.814 for MWU, 0.904 for GSW, and 3.543 for Bernoulli assignment.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest adding higher-order covariate terms and interactions, or using kernel methods, to address nonlinear outcome-covariate relationships. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future research could evaluate the design in prospective experiments and under operational constraints such as fixed treatment counts, stratification requirements, or limited randomization. narrate.summary: This paper presents a sequential method for choosing experiments to improve a later decision, rather than focusing only on learning unknown model parameters. It introduces Decision Utility Gain (DUG), which measures how much an experiment is expected to improve the utility of the best decision. The proposed Transformer Neural Decision Process (TNDP) combines a design-selection policy with a prediction model in one architecture, and trains the policy using rewards that account for future steps. The authors evaluate the method on simulated prediction and treatment-selection tasks, public hyperparameter benchmark data, and a retrosynthesis task. Across the reported comparisons, the method improves decision or optimization utility over the tested alternatives and makes design selection rapidly after training.
narrate.key_results: In decision-aware active learning, TNDP achieved a higher proportion of correct decisions across 10 design steps than random sampling, uncertainty sampling, decision-uncertainty sampling, targeted-information sampling, and decision expected-information-gain sampling; the evaluation used 100 test points. On four hyperparameter benchmark search spaces, TNDP achieved the best reported utility among the methods compared, with 50 design steps, an initial set of 5 points, and a goal of selecting 3 configurations. In the active-learning timing comparison, TNDP required an average of 0.015 seconds to select one design and 0.31 seconds for 10 rounds, compared with 572 and 5,746 seconds for decision expected-information-gain sampling and 1,558 and 15,613 seconds for targeted-information sampling. For retrosynthesis, TNDP outperformed random search on 50 held-out molecules, but the paper reports no exact utility values in its text.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for constructing response surface experiments when treatment combinations cannot be freely randomized because of nested or crossed unit structures. It targets estimation of fixed response-model parameters while also allowing pure error and lack-of-fit assessment, without requiring prior estimates of variance components. The method optimizes the design one stratum at a time, holding earlier-stratum factor settings fixed and using point exchanges within each stratum. Compound criteria let experimenters balance estimation, inference, and lack-of-fit assessment. Four examples show that useful designs can be constructed for row-column, split-row-column, strip-split-plot, and split-row-split-column layouts, including a 500-run example.
narrate.key_results: In the pastry example, the compromise design had 93.23% D-optimality efficiency and 90.67% A-optimality efficiency relative to the JMP design when both variance ratios were 1; it provided 7 pure error and 2 lack-of-fit degrees of freedom in the run stratum. In the protein extraction example, the compromise design had 86.56% D-optimality efficiency and 84.21% A-optimality efficiency relative to the JMP design when both variance ratios were 1, and provided 7 pure error degrees of freedom in the day stratum and 6 in the run stratum. In the strip-split-plot example, the compromise design achieved 98.54% D-optimality efficiency and 91.26% A-optimality efficiency relative to the best fixed-effects design at variance ratios of 1, while providing pure error degrees of freedom in each of the three treatment-bearing strata. In the 500-run coating example, the compromise design achieved 90.96% D-optimality efficiency and 96.44% A-optimality efficiency relative to the D-optimal design at variance ratios of 1, and provided 2, 1, and 39 pure error degrees of freedom in the batches, batch-by-occasion, and run strata, respectively; the authors could not obtain a JMP comparison design for this example.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a way to choose which language-model generation pairs should receive human preference labels in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). It assumes that rewards are linear in known generation embeddings and that pairwise preferences follow the Bradley-Terry model. Its method, Optimal Design for Policy Optimization (ODPO), uses optimal design to select informative pairs from a fixed candidate dataset before collecting labels. It estimates rewards from the resulting comparisons and uses the estimates to select the best generation for each prompt. The authors prove upper and lower bounds on simple regret that match up to constant and logarithmic factors; they do not report an empirical experiment.
narrate.key_results: For a design approximating the optimal design within a factor of 3/2, with regularization set to 1/d, the authors bound expected simple regret by a term that scales as 30 times the square root of (d+2)/T times a logarithmic factor, plus 31 divided by the square root of T. Their lower bound is d times exp(-5) divided by 4 times the square root of T, for d at least 16 and T at least d squared, showing agreement in rate up to constants and logarithmic factors. The upper bound applies to arbitrary candidate action sets under the paper’s assumptions, and the lower bound establishes a worst-case limit for any algorithm. These are theoretical results, not empirical comparisons with other selection methods.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their guarantees rely on a linear reward model, Bradley-Terry pairwise preferences, and bounded embeddings and reward parameters. narrate.summary: This paper presents CoDiff, a method for Bayesian optimal experimental design that selects experiments to maximize expected information gain about unknown parameters. It is designed for both models with explicit probability densities and settings where the prior is available only through samples, including diffusion-model priors. The method combines a pooled posterior distribution, used to represent information from possible outcomes, with a new information-gain gradient and a single loop that updates the design and samples together. The authors evaluate it using simulated sequential source localization and a handwritten-image reconstruction task based on MNIST. They report better information and parameter estimates than the compared methods in source localization, and better image reconstruction than random design in the image task.
narrate.key_results: In source localization, the method used 200 samples for each of the two sampling groups, 400 samples total, and each measurement step took 2.9 seconds; results were summarized over 100 rollouts. The authors report a 30% improvement over the reinforcement-learning comparison on sequential prior contrastive estimation, a higher sequential nested Monte Carlo bound, and an L2 Wasserstein distance two orders of magnitude lower than the alternatives. For image reconstruction, median structural similarity scores after experiments 1 through 6 were 0.227, 0.338, 0.528, 0.673, 0.789, and 0.826 for the proposed method, versus 0.168, 0.275, 0.350, 0.391, 0.421, and 0.463 for random designs. The image design steps took about 7.3 seconds each.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method in real experiments and across additional public datasets, while assessing robustness to model misspecification and practical restrictions on allowable designs. narrate.summary: The paper presents a software workflow for optimizing complex manufacturing processes, tested on MicroLED production using experimental data. The objective is to predict process outputs and find input recipes that improve one or more targets, including maxWPE. The workflow standardizes and cleans experimental data, reduces the number of input parameters, trains predictive models, and searches those models for candidate recipes. For multiple output targets, it presents candidate solutions as a Pareto front so process engineers can choose tradeoffs. The authors report that the workflow was applied to real process data and describe model-fit results, but do not quantify improvements achieved in follow-up experiments.
narrate.key_results: The reported dataset contains 20,600 input parameters and 2 output parameters. Automatic reduction selected 20 parameters, after which process experts excluded 5 based on their physical knowledge. For a deep neural network example assuming independent objectives, the reported coefficient-of-determination scores were 0.97 and 0.93 on training data, and 0.87 and 0.65 on test data, for maxWPE and Lambda peak respectively. The paper also demonstrates two-target candidate selection with a Pareto front and dashboards for inspecting solution performance, quality, stability, and exploration-versus-exploitation tradeoffs; it does not provide a numerical comparison against another optimization method.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors describe optimization from experimental raw data as challenging because the data are highly variable and dense. They also identify balancing physical intuition with holistic optimization, and building a platform accessible to non-specialists, as challenges.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper does not report the number of experimental runs, a quantitative comparison with a conventional design-of-experiments method, or measured outcomes from the recipes tested after optimization. The data are obfuscated, and parameter selection and recipe review depend partly on expert judgment, which limits independent reproduction and makes it difficult to assess how well the workflow transfers to other processes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose future research on Bayesian optimization using surrogate models, reinforcement controls, optimal control policies, and sequence-based neural networks for time-series data. They also plan to adapt more sophisticated optimization strategies for more than three objectives.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a prospective comparison of the proposed workflow with established experimental-design and optimization approaches, reporting both the number of runs required and the resulting process improvements. Further work could also test the workflow's reproducibility across processes and assess how recipe constraints and expert review affect the selected solutions.

It extends Control Using Predictions as Covariates (CUPAC), which adjusts for predictions based on pre-experiment information, by adding a linear adjustment for selected in-experiment covariates. The method selects covariates using treatment-control mean-balance tests, alongside domain knowledge, and requires mean equivalence for the selected variables. The authors derive consistency and asymptotic normality results and provide a consistent variance estimator. In Etsy experiments, the approach improved prediction and produced additional variance reduction beyond the existing CUPAC pipeline.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used 29 Etsy experiments with customer conversion rate as the primary outcome. The CUPAC baseline used 117 pre-experiment covariates, while the proposed second-stage adjustment used 23 selected in-experiment covariates. The reported prediction improvement over CUPAC ranged from 0.02 to over 0.14 across experiments. The authors report additional variance reduction beyond CUPAC across the experiments, and compare the overall variance reduction with the difference-in-means estimator; they do not give a single numerical summary of those variance reductions in the text.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that a large p-value in the balance tests does not prove mean equivalence; it may reflect limited power, and the screening should be combined with domain knowledge. They also state that finite-sample selection depends on test power, multiplicity, and the chosen significance level, and that a full semiparametric efficiency analysis is beyond the paper's scope.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation covers experiments from one company, over one month, and the treatments and data are anonymized, so it does not establish performance across other industries or experiment types. The paper does not report the experiment sample sizes or a single numerical aggregate for the variance gains, and mean-balance screening alone cannot establish that a covariate is causally unaffected by treatment in every relevant way.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest that further gains may come from identifying additional informative post-treatment covariates through richer domain expertise or data-driven methods such as machine learning. They also describe nonlinear second-stage adjustment and a single prediction model using both pre-experiment and in-experiment data as possible generalizations.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the method prospectively in experiments across different organizations and intervention types, reporting sample sizes and uncertainty around the estimated gains. It could also assess selection procedures based on practically meaningful equivalence bounds and develop deployment guidance for monitoring covariate balance and estimator performance over time.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a framework for sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design in dynamic systems described by partial differential equations with uncertain, high-dimensional parameters. Its objective is to select experiments adaptively to maximize expected information gain about those parameters. The framework combines a terminal formulation of the design objective with posterior approximations and a latent attention neural operator that predicts both system observations and their derivatives. The authors test it on simulated tumor growth, choosing four MRI observation days from ten candidate days. In that example, the method reduces uncertainty and achieves a reported amortized computational speedup of 180 times compared with finite element calculations.
narrate.key_results: For the tumor model, the parameter and full-state observation each had 14,003 dimensions; the authors reduced both to 64 dimensions with reported projection errors below 1%. Across the evaluated time points, the latent attention neural operator's observation prediction error decreased from 8.05% to 2.27%, and its reduced Jacobian error ranged from 4.05% to 1.57%; the neural ordinary differential equation's recursive observation error reached 95.91% at day 10, while the projected neural network's error reached 89.65% at day 6. The operator's mean relative error for maximum a posteriori estimates was 1.52% for daily observations and 1.31% for the sparse observation set, and the reported mean relative eigenvalue error was 0.8%. For information-gain evaluation, its online calculation took 16.0 seconds versus 3,148.9 seconds with the finite element method, a 197-times speedup; including offline data generation and training, the authors report an amortized 180-times speedup. The selected adaptive observation days were 2, 7, 9, and 10, compared with days 2, 8, 9, and 10 for the static design and days 2, 4, 6, and 8 for the uniform design; the adaptive design produced the smallest reported parameter uncertainty in this simulated example.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that their approach may be less suitable when the posterior is not well approximated by a Laplace approximation or when the posterior covariance is not low rank. They identify variational inference as a possible approach for those cases.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is limited to one simulated tumor-growth application with a specified model, prior, and observation setup, so the reported performance does not establish accuracy for real MRI data or other physical systems. The surrogate requires costly offline basis construction, simulation data, Jacobian generation, and training, and the paper does not evaluate how these costs change under practical imaging constraints or model mismatch.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring variational inference when Laplace approximation is inadequate or the posterior covariance is not low rank. They also identify extensions to selecting observation locations as well as times, use of greedy or swapping-greedy optimization, and adaptive refinement of the neural network to predict beyond its training horizon.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the method with real clinical imaging data and compare its selected schedules with operational constraints such as available scan windows and patient burden. It could also test robustness to errors in the tumor model and observation-noise assumptions, and validate whether the reported uncertainty reduction carries over to outcomes relevant to clinical decisions.

narrate.summary: Inspection-Guided Randomization (IGR) is a framework for restricting the treatment assignments available in a randomized experiment. It is designed for experiments with different objectives and estimands, including trials with interference and experiments that form groups with specified compositions. Researchers define design desiderata, translate them into inspection metrics, combine the metrics into a fitness score, and filter a pool of candidate assignments. They evaluate and adapt the resulting design, pre-register accepted assignments and their probabilities, and then randomly select an assignment for the experiment. Simulations show that this approach can improve estimation relative to benchmark randomization designs, although the gains depend on the chosen metrics and restrictions.
narrate.key_results: In the interference simulation, the researchers enumerated 100,000 candidate allocations and retained 500, the top 0.5 percent by fitness score. With mirror allocations included and interference weighted at 0.75, the difference-in-means estimator’s absolute bias was 88.31 percent of the CR benchmark’s, with reported variation of 0.56 percentage points; at an interference weight of 1, it was 86.18 percent, with variation of 0.37 percentage points. At an interference weight of 0.125, the difference-in-means variance was 0.003, compared with 0.61 for the CR benchmark; at a weight of 0.875, it rose to 1.01. In the group-formation simulation, IGR with balance and composition criteria reduced RMSE to 56.82, 55.52, and 56.39 percent of the group-formation-randomization benchmark across the three group comparisons using the maximum Mahalanobis criterion; using the sum of maximum absolute standardized mean differences reduced it to 48.83, 47.61, and 47.82 percent.

key_equations.name: Weighted fitness score in the interference example
key_equations.explanation: The fitness score f for allocation z and covariate matrix X is a weighted sum of the fraction of control participants exposed to treatment through network neighbors, m with the FracExpo label, and the Mahalanobis balance metric, m with the Mahalanobis label.

key_equations.name: IGR assignment mechanism
key_equations.explanation: The probability under the IGR assignment mechanism P_IGR of drawing allocation z is p_z when z is in the candidate pool Z_pool and passes restriction rule r applied to fitness score f using covariates X; otherwise its probability is zero.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that IGR uses a hand-crafted fitness function, which may be an imperfect proxy for the true conditional mean-squared error. They also emphasize that choosing and evaluating appropriate metrics and restrictions requires substantial analyst and domain-expert effort, and that flawed choices may produce poor designs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The reported performance evidence comes from simulations rather than a real experiment, and the interference results rely on a particular simulated network and exposure model. The examples use 100,000 candidate allocations and a 0.5 percent acceptance threshold, so the paper does not establish how well the approach scales or performs when the candidate pool misses important assignments or real-world constraints limit feasible randomization.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing theory about how closely the fitness function must approximate conditional mean-squared error to improve estimates. They also suggest using pilot studies, earlier waves, or historical experiments to refine the fitness function, and developing accessible implementation software, potentially with an interactive dashboard.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs in real experiments and assess their sensitivity to misspecified interference networks, exposure thresholds, and outcome models. It could also develop and evaluate ways to incorporate practical constraints, such as treatment-delivery capacity or participant availability, while retaining a sufficiently broad set of randomized assignments.

narrate.summary: The paper presents Interactive Design of Experiments (IDoE), an interactive approach for optimizing an air-conditioning (AC) system whose simulation is too complex to invert directly. It combines an initial space-filling sample, a deep learning (DL) model that estimates control settings for desired system outputs, and numerical simulations that check those estimates. Engineers use an interactive pressure-enthalpy diagram and linked plots to set targets, inspect results, and guide additional runs near promising settings. The authors demonstrate the approach on an automotive cooling-system model with five control parameters. In the example, the team improved the coefficient of performance while refining the solution over three iterations.
narrate.key_results: The initial sample called for 5,000 simulation runs, of which 4,182 produced valid results; each run took about 10 seconds, and producing the initial sample took about 14 hours. For an iteration, the engineers ran 20 simulations with parameters varied by up to 5% around the values predicted by the DL model. In the showcased scenario, the coefficient of performance improved over the starting case, and a promising configuration was identified in three iterations. The learned model reported a test-set mean squared error of 0.25. Domain experts reported that the approach could reduce work taking several days to a few hours, or at least an order of magnitude faster; the paper does not report a controlled comparison against another design method.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that parallel coordinates are practical for about a dozen control parameters and that simulations must be fast enough to produce refinements; waiting a few minutes for 20 runs was acceptable to their engineers, but longer waits may not be. They also acknowledge that the user interface is complex and could be improved.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation centers on one automotive cooling-system model and one described optimization scenario, so it does not establish performance across other systems, objectives, or operating conditions. The paper reports a test error for the learned model but does not provide a controlled comparison of optimization quality, robustness, or convergence against alternative design methods.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using advances such as deep learning to speed up simulation solvers, adding more constraints to the design goals used for predictions, supporting exploration outside the default control-parameter space, and developing an interface that adapts to users’ needs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the approach across multiple cooling-system models and target scenarios, using controlled comparisons that measure simulation effort and solution quality. It could also assess how uncertainty in the inverse predictions affects the choice of refinement runs and how the method performs when practical manufacturing or operating constraints are added.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an online framework for choosing among candidate adaptive treatment-allocation designs during an experiment. It targets the mean primary outcome that would be expected if participants had been assigned under each candidate design, using their observed design contexts. The framework estimates these outcomes with targeted maximum likelihood estimation and selects the candidate with the highest lower confidence bound. Its motivating application compares adaptive designs that use short-term surrogate outcomes to guide treatment assignment while the long-term outcome is still being collected. Simulations show that the framework can favor early or later surrogates as their value changes over time, while providing estimates with approximately nominal confidence-interval coverage.
narrate.key_results: In the main simulations, the authors compared seven designs over 500 runs, with 50 enrollment times and 50 participants enrolled at each time; treatment probabilities were capped at 90%. At time 50 in Scenario 2, the proposed design's average regret was 0.025, close to 0.024 for the design using the best early surrogate and below 0.120 for equal-probability randomization. In Scenario 1, its regret was 0.080 at time 50, compared with 0.071 for the best fixed candidate; the proposed design's regret became second-lowest from time 23. In simulations inspired by the ADAPT-R trial, using data from 215 participants to generate outcomes and 500 simulated runs, the final expected outcome was 0.576 for the proposed design, compared with 0.579 for the best fixed early-surrogate design and 0.565 for equal-probability randomization. Across the reported simulation settings, the estimator generally had low bias and confidence-interval coverage near the nominal 95% level.

key_equations.name: Online candidate selection
key_equations.explanation: At time t, j*_t is the candidate design j with the largest lower confidence bound, using its estimated value Ψ-hat, estimated standard error σ-hat, sample size n_t, confidence-level quantile z, and tail probability α.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their context-specific target is an approximation to the ideal value under the full sequence of data that a candidate design would generate, and that the ideal target is more computationally intensive to estimate. They say the approximation is most accurate when observed contexts represent those the candidate design would induce, and their causal identification and inference rely on stated exchangeability, positivity, and regularity conditions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations use a limited set of outcome structures and candidate designs, so performance when treatment effects, enrollment patterns, or surrogate relationships differ substantially remains uncertain. The application based on ADAPT-R is a simulation informed by trial data rather than a prospective implementation, and the method's reliance on adequate treatment assignment probabilities and representative observed contexts may be difficult to satisfy in some operational trials.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further study of the computationally intensive ideal estimand, including its strengths and limitations relative to the context-specific estimand and the trade-offs between statistical properties and computational efficiency.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the method prospectively in clinical or online experiments and test it under realistic operational constraints, including uneven enrollment, missing outcomes, and restricted treatment availability. It could also examine sequential safeguards against unstable early selection and compare alternative selection criteria or candidate-library construction strategies.

narrate.summary: This article surveys optimal experimental design: methods for deciding what data to collect to support estimation, prediction, or other goals. It covers classical criteria for linear models as well as Bayesian and decision-based criteria that apply to nonlinear and non-Gaussian models. The authors review ways to estimate design criteria and optimize designs, including Monte Carlo, density approximation, dimension reduction, combinatorial selection, and continuous optimization. They also explain sequential design policies that adapt later experiments to earlier observations while accounting for future experiments. The article synthesizes methods and open challenges rather than proposing one new design algorithm or reporting a single winning design.
narrate.key_results: The review reports that the standard nested Monte Carlo approach to estimating expected information gain has a mean-square error rate of order computational budget to the power negative two-thirds; reaching mean-square error equal to tolerance squared requires effort of order tolerance to the power negative three. It contrasts this with multilevel nested Monte Carlo, which is reported to reduce the effort to order tolerance to the power negative two. The article also describes a linear-Gaussian example where finite-sample bias in the standard estimator obscures the true best design, while multiple importance sampling performs better without guaranteeing stable maxima at finite sample sizes. These are results from methods and studies covered by the review, not a head-to-head evaluation conducted by the authors.

key_equations.name: Expected utility design criterion
key_equations.explanation: The expected utility U for design xi averages the utility u over observations Y and parameters Theta under the model for that design.

key_equations.name: Information gain in parameters
key_equations.explanation: The mutual information I between observations Y and parameters Theta for design xi is the expected logarithm of the likelihood density divided by the marginal observation density p.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that computational evaluation of design criteria can be difficult, particularly for nonlinear or high-dimensional models, expensive simulations, and implicit models. They also explicitly say that their discussion of variational bounds is not comprehensive, and note that full information-gain design for nonlinear infinite-dimensional problems has not, to their knowledge, been realized, in part because of computational and theoretical challenges.
narrate.limitations_unstated: As a broad survey, the article does not establish a systematic review protocol or provide a common benchmark for comparing the many methods it discusses. The methods are often supported by different assumptions and examples, so the review does not establish how well their reported advantages transfer to a particular quality-engineering application or to experiments with model misspecification and operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify open questions and challenges as a motivation for the survey and include an Outlook section. The supplied text does not include the specific proposals in that section.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be standardized comparisons of design methods on realistic experiments, including sensitivity to incorrect models and prior assumptions, run costs, and practical randomization constraints. Further work could also develop reusable software and validation studies that link sequential design policies to implementation and outcomes in real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops Constrained Row Screening (CRowS), a method for screening many compounds by placing pools of compounds in wells while limiting the number in each well. It targets supersaturated designs for a main-effects model in which the number of compounds can equal or exceed the number of wells. The design is constructed to reduce the average squared off-diagonal values of its information matrix, subject to the pool-size limit, using a coordinate-exchange search. The observed responses are analyzed with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) to identify active compounds. Simulations favor CRowS over one-compound-one-well screening and the existing poolHiTS method, and laboratory experiments identify a known inhibitor in three of four screens.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, CRowS had higher true positive rates than one-compound-one-well screening and poolHiTS across the design settings studied, while poolHiTS often had difficulty controlling false positive rates. The compared pooled designs used 88 to 99 wells to screen 96 to 192 compounds, whereas one-compound-one-well screening used one well per compound. The authors constructed designs using 100 randomized algorithm starts and selected the best criterion value. In the laboratory demonstration with 31 compounds, CRowS identified the known inhibitor in three of four experiments, including the experiment allowing 10 compounds per well; it missed the inhibitor when the limit was five per well.
